items.name: RSI-Exam: Measuring Recursive Self-Improvement on Long-Horizon, Executable Research Tasks
items.one_liner: 88 executable research tasks (35 public / 53 private) across 6 domains; agent gets up to 12h on a visible split, submission is replayed once from scratch on a sealed split and that single number is the score.
items.why_relevant: The canonical Sept-2026 'RSI' benchmark. Scores normalized 0.00 (inherited baseline) to 0.60 (frontier-calibrated reference): Opus 5 0.464, GPT-5.6 0.433, GLM 5.3 0.403, Kimi K3 0.382, Grok 4.6 0.367. Visible-to-hidden decay is 11.7-24.7% for every model, i.e. a large fraction of 'self-improvement' is overfitting to the dev split. Site: https://rsi-exam.ai

items.name: AI4AI-Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agents in Algorithmic Design for Recursive Self-Improvement
items.one_liner: 10 frozen research repos across 10 training-algorithm families; 4h on one B300 to rewrite the learning algorithm, rerun from scratch up to 12h, scored by hidden evaluator on a 0-1 scale (0.1 = original algorithm).
items.why_relevant: Directly operationalizes RSI as 'improve the process that produces AI'. Mean 0.166 across 29 configs of 6 systems, best 0.250: agents close under a fifth of the baseline-to-optimum gap. Agents that actually modify the learning mechanism score 0.226 vs 0.126; more reasoning raises willingness to modify algorithms from 8% to 64% of submissions. Explicitly isolates algorithm changes from hyperparameter tuning (positioned as rigorous successor to autoresearch).

items.name: PostTrainBench
items.one_liner: Measures how well CLI agents (Claude Code, Codex CLI) can post-train base LLMs on a single H100 in 10 hours, scored on 7 downstream benchmarks (reasoning, tool use, knowledge, math, health, code).
items.why_relevant: The 'AI improves AI' benchmark with the most traction; finding that data assembly and initialization remain the largest levers (data-centric, not algorithmic gains), which AI4AI-Bench cites as the gap it fills.

items.name: SEAGym: An Evaluation Environment for Self-Evolving LLM Agents
items.one_liner: Tsinghua. Turns Harbor-compatible benchmarks (Terminal-Bench 2.0, HLE) into self-evolution task streams with train batches, frozen update-validation, held-out ID/OOD views, replay diagnostics, snapshot + cost records; compares ACE, TF-GRPO, AHE under a shared epoch/batch protocol.
items.why_relevant: Core methodological point: a single sequential curve hides whether an update is reusable, overfits recent tasks, raises cost, or harms old behavior. Findings: frequent updates often fail to improve held-out performance, useful intermediate snapshots can collapse later, and source diversity / model backend change harness reliability. Repo: https://github.com/antropy-research/SEAGym

items.name: SEA-Eval: A Benchmark for Evaluating Self-Evolving Agents Beyond Episodic Assessment
items.one_liner: Fudan. Formalizes the Self-Evolving Agent and 'Evolutionary Flywheel'; sequential task streams measure evolutionary gain, stability, and implicit alignment convergence with Success Rate and Token consumption as co-primary metrics.
items.why_relevant: Introduces the 'pseudo-evolution' vs genuine evolution distinction: frameworks with identical success rates differ up to ~30x (31.2x per-task) in tokens; only architectures with effective experience distillation show monotonic token convergence. Argues success rate alone creates a 'capability illusion'.

items.name: EvoHarnessBench: Can Your Agents Keep Pace with an Evolving Harness?
items.one_liner: Salesforce/UNC (Zixuan Ke, Mohit Bansal, Shafiq Joty). 17 multi-stage harness streams, 802 tasks, 520 tools, 42 skills, 62 agents; non-stationarity is placed in the harness itself rather than the task stream.
items.why_relevant: Names 'harness-induced forgetting': harness expansion alone degrades performance on previously solved tasks. Adaptation gains are inconsistent across evolution stages, and retention and adaptation pull in different directions. Directly relevant to any framework that keeps adding skills/tools.

items.name: HarnessDev: Can LLMs Create and Evolve Their Own Agent Harness?
items.one_liner: Shifts the unit of evaluation to runnable infrastructure: Creation (from minimal seed + few cases) then Evolution (revise own harness from downstream feedback); 6 creator LLMs, 4 domains, 5 downstream benchmarks, 2,207 instances, capability + token cost.
items.why_relevant: Generated harnesses trail human-engineered references on code and search/research, match or exceed on writing and ML experimentation. Evolution gains exist but are unstable, transfer only partially to held-out tasks, and depend strongly on the model executing the harness (limited cross-model transfer).

items.name: MemEvoBench: Benchmarking Memory MisEvolution in LLM Agents
items.one_liner: First benchmark for long-horizon memory safety under adversarial memory injection, noisy tool outputs, and biased feedback: QA tasks over 7 domains / 36 risk types plus workflow tasks from 20 Agent-SafetyBench environments with mixed benign/misleading memory pools.
items.why_relevant: Shows memory evolution itself is a major contributor to safety degradation and that static prompt defenses are insufficient; establishes 'misevolution' as a failure class self-improving loops must measure. Repo: https://github.com/xiewwee11/MemEvoBench

items.name: Practice Makes Unsafe: Skill Misevolution in Self-Improving LLM Agents (SkillMisevo-Gym / SkillMisevo-Bench)
items.one_liner: Lifecycle-aware harness that versions skill state across 4 agent frameworks and 6 evolution methods; frozen benchmark from malicious exposure to carryover tasks with concept-aligned benign tasks and 9 lifecycle metrics; 25 configs x 525 tasks x 25 episodes.
items.why_relevant: All 21 evolved configurations author unsafe artifacts; 15 reach fresh-session harm. Unsafe success becomes reusable policy after the triggering input is gone because evolution optimizes outcomes, not procedure safety. SafeEvolve wrapper cuts unsafe retrieval / fresh-session harm by 26.7 / 17.3 pp at 0.4-pt utility cost.

items.name: FinEvo-Bench: A Longitudinal Benchmark for Self-Evolving Agents in Professional Financial Workflows
items.one_liner: 120 real-case-grounded multi-file tasks in 20 business scenes across 6 financial domains; each scene has 6 related cases sharing a professional procedure and reviewed rubric; interleaved streams with state-reset controls isolate cross-task self-evolution gain.
items.why_relevant: A paired (evolution on/off, state-reset) protocol is the pattern the critique papers demand; open-ended outputs scored for quality and compliance rather than pass/fail.

items.name: Do Agent Optimizers Compound? A Continual-Learning Evaluation on Terminal-Bench 2.0
items.one_liner: RELAI tech report (Wang, Kattakinda, Feizi). Two-phase continual evaluation on hard Terminal-Bench 2.0 tasks comparing GEPA, Meta Harness, and RELAI-VCL under identical optimization budgets.
items.why_relevant: All three beat baseline in the static one-shot setting; once new tasks arrive they diverge: GEPA transfers below the unoptimized baseline, Meta Harness transfers but cannot improve with a second budget, only RELAI-VCL compounds (lifelong avg pass 76.4% vs 66.0 GEPA, 64.6 Meta Harness, 58.7 baseline). Vendor-authored, but the phase-2 protocol is the point. Artifacts: https://github.com/relai-ai/Continual-Learning-Terminal-Bench

items.name: Adaptive Auto-Harness: Sustained Self-Improvement for Agentic System Deployment on Open-Ended Task Streams
items.one_liner: Emory/Amazon/PSU/UIUC. Shows a single densely-updated harness (A-Evolve, GEPA, Meta-Harness style) is brittle on open-ended streams: accuracy peaks early then declines; proposes decomposing gap into evolution vs adaptation loss with a harness tree and solve-time routing.
items.why_relevant: Documents the peak-then-decay curve that fixed-benchmark evaluations never show; argues heterogeneous streams need multiple harnesses plus routing rather than one monolithic evolving harness.

items.name: Rethinking the Evaluation of Harness Evolution for Agents
items.one_liner: AI2 / UW (Hajishirzi, Tsvetkov, Dasigi, Teng Xiao). Argues harness evolution is an iterative search and must be compared with task-level search baselines under matched feedback and inference budgets, on held-out tasks rather than the search benchmark.
items.why_relevant: The most-cited critique: on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with GPT-5.4 and Claude Opus 4.6, automatic harness evolution does not consistently outperform simple test-time scaling and shows limited generalization. Reported gains risk being 'more search' plus overfitting to the public benchmark used for both search and eval.

items.name: Simple Baselines are Competitive with Code Evolution (Gideoni, Risi, Gal; ICLR 2026)
items.one_liner: Two trivial baselines match or exceed sophisticated LLM code-evolution pipelines on mathematical bounds, agentic scaffold design, and ML competitions.
items.why_relevant: Establishes that search space and domain knowledge in the prompt, not the evolution pipeline, dictate the performance ceiling; explicitly calls for more rigorous evaluation of self-improving/evolutionary systems. This is the 'trivial-baselines' paper the critique wave builds on.

items.name: What Do Evolutionary Coding Agents Evolve? (EvoTrace / EvoReplay)
items.one_liner: Pelleriti, Pokutta et al. EvoTrace: structured traces (programs, parent-child graph, prompts, scores, evaluator metadata) over 4 evolutionary frameworks and 16 math/algorithm tasks; EvoReplay reconstructs local search states and runs controlled interventions.
items.why_relevant: Separates gains from new algorithmic structure vs constant re-tuning vs recombination vs evaluator overfitting. Most score gains come from a small subset of edit types, and ~30% of lines added during search are byte-identical re-introductions of previously deleted lines. Mechanism auditing, not best-score, is the takeaway.

items.name: Harness Updating Is Not Harness Benefit: Disentangling Evolution Capabilities in Self-Evolving LLM Agents
items.one_liner: Minhua Lin + 16 (PSU/Amazon et al.). Splits self-evolution into harness-updating (produce useful persistent updates) and harness-benefit (gain from them at solve time).
items.why_relevant: Harness-updating is flat across model tiers (Qwen3.5-9B produces updates comparable to Claude Opus 4.6); harness-benefit is non-monotonic, peaking at mid-tier models and shrinking for strong models. Implication: the evolving model and the executing model should be chosen separately, and strong-model results understate/overstate harness value.

items.name: Are Online Skill and Memory Modules Always Worth Their Tokens? A Budget-Constrained Study of Web Agents
items.one_liner: Re-evaluates online skill and workflow-memory modules under a fixed total inference budget across 3 WebArena domains and 3 models (Gemini 3 Flash, GPT-5.4-mini, Qwen 3.6-27B), plus WorkArena-L1.
items.why_relevant: Vanilla actor matches or beats all three augmentation methods in aggregate success while often using fewer tokens; apparent gains vanish against a budget-matched actor. Cost accounting is a first-order evaluation requirement.

items.name: Demystifying Agent Skills: Why They Work - Until They Don't
items.one_liner: 528 paired triples across SkillsBench (144), Terminal-Bench 2.0 (186), Terminal-Bench-Pro (198); controlled study of representation, outcome annotation, retrieval difficulty, cross-framework robustness.
items.why_relevant: Skills work mainly as procedural anchors (65.7% of successes) not knowledge injection (4.5%); retrieval precision collapses from 29.6% (5-skill pool) to 3.3% (100-skill pool); skills fail under brittle assumptions or incompatible contexts. Warns that growing skill libraries in self-evolving loops self-sabotage via retrieval. Repo: https://github.com/zhiyuanjiang04/demystify-agent-skills

items.name: SkillsBench: Benchmarking How Well Agent Skills Work Across Diverse Tasks
items.one_liner: 87 tasks across 8 domains with curated skills and deterministic verifiers; paper arXiv 2602.12670.
items.why_relevant: The reference substrate for skill studies: curated skills raise pass rate 33.9% -> 50.5% (+16.6 pp), which sets the bar that self-generated/evolved skills are then measured against (CTA finds +0.3 pp on SWE-Skills-Bench).

items.name: Counterfactual Trace Auditing of LLM Agent Skills
items.one_liner: Pairs each with-skill trace against a without-skill trace on the same task, segments and aligns goal-directed phases, emits structured Skill Influence Pattern annotations describing behavioral effect rather than only outcome.
items.why_relevant: On SWE-Skills-Bench with Claude across 49 tasks, pass rate moved only +0.3 pp on average, yet behavior changed substantively. Gives a template for auditing whether an evolved artifact actually altered agent behavior, not just the aggregate score.

items.name: Evo-Bench: Can Language Models Improve Agent Harness?
items.one_liner: RUC / Nanbeige. 608 harness-sensitive tasks from 5 benchmarks across Search, Office, General; long-horizon protocol measures whether a model can diagnose, rewrite and improve an executable harness while isolating harness gains from base-model strength and preventing task overfit.
items.why_relevant: Top of 9 frontier/open models gain up to 16.6 absolute points, approaching human-engineered baselines; treats harness-evolving as a measurable model capability. Repo: https://github.com/RUCAIBox/Evo-Bench

items.name: HarnessOpt-Bench: Evaluating LLMs at Harness Optimization
items.one_liner: Scale AI. Optimizer LLM receives a seed harness, graded feedback, and a fixed target-evaluation budget; nominated candidate scored by normalized gain over seed on a held-out test partition under expensive, stochastic evaluation.
items.why_relevant: Explicitly budgets evaluations and scores on held-out partitions (the two fixes the AI2 critique asks for); reveals substantial variation across models and tasks.

items.name: EvoAgentBench: Benchmarking Agent Self-Evolution via Ability Transfer
items.one_liner: Ability Graph where edges are shared reusable procedures (search strategy, debugging routine, validation workflow); 1006 train + 367 test tasks over web research, algorithmic reasoning, SWE, knowledge work.
items.why_relevant: Isolates procedural transfer specifically, the mechanism most self-evolution frameworks claim. Repo: https://github.com/EverMind-AI/EvoAgentBench

items.name: PAST-Bench: Benchmarking the Foundations of Recursive Self-Improvement in Personal Agents
items.one_liner: Gen-Verse (Mengdi Wang, Ling Yang). 26 scenarios / 204 episodes of fresh-session task sequences with retained experience toggled on/off under matched conditions; 7 base models x 4 frameworks.
items.why_relevant: Improvement from retained experience is real but uneven across memory, procedural reuse, information gathering and update; the on/off matched-condition design is the minimal causal test for 'does experience help'. Repo: https://github.com/Gen-Verse/PAST-Bench

items.name: GDPevo: Evaluating Agent Self-Evolution on Real Business Tasks
items.one_liner: Evolution-native benchmark with 'rule hybridization': atomic business rules distributed across 5 train tasks and recombined in 5 held-out tests per group (120 tasks, 12 groups; CRM/ERP/finance/healthcare/legal).
items.why_relevant: Makes test-time gains attributable to what was learned; self-evolution adds up to +16.44 pp held-out accuracy but best evolved agents remain far below the 91.6% fully-informed oracle. Repo: https://github.com/Prism-Shadow/GDPevo

items.name: AIDE²: First Evidence of Recursive Self-Improvement (Weco AI)
items.one_liner: Outer loop (Opus 4.7) rewrote the inner autoresearch agent's harness for 100 iterations over 8 days (~90% rejected, 7 survivors); AIDE85 beat the 2-year hand-tuned baseline on held-out MLE-Bench Lite, ALE-Bench Lite, WeatherBench 2, KernelBench; reward hacking on KernelBench fell 63% -> 34%.
items.why_relevant: The hottest RSI claim of summer 2026 and the empirical foil for the critique papers. Self-reported, no peer review; authors concede no 'ignition' (discovered agent did not improve the outer loop) and no evidence of takeoff. Discovered: bandit search with fork-on-stall, 16x context compression, 3-layer anti-reward-hacking.

items.name: karpathy/autoresearch
items.one_liner: AI agents running research on single-GPU nanochat training automatically; modify -> verify -> keep/discard loop.
items.why_relevant: The cultural substrate for the 2026 RSI wave; AI4AI-Bench and RSI-Exam position themselves as rigorous successors (full repos, hidden evaluators, algorithm-vs-hyperparameter isolation). Spawned thousands of derivative loops (AutoResearchClaw 14.4k, pi-autoresearch 8k, darwin-skill 6k).

items.name: AI's recursive self-improvement might not come so quickly after all (MIT Technology Review)
items.one_liner: Covers a Princeton study (Kapoor et al.) giving Claude Opus 4.8 six days and $3,000 to reproduce two unpublished NeurIPS 2026 papers: engineering completed, papers rejected for lacking novelty and bizarre experimental choices.
items.why_relevant: Sets the skeptical mainstream framing: agents are 'unambiguously bad at carrying out the research itself'; Jack Clark calls lack of creativity a bearish signal on short RSI timelines. Bottlenecks named: exploring alternatives, backtracking, resource management.

items.name: Recursive Self-Improvement in AI: From Bounded Self-Refinement to Autonomous Research Loops
items.one_liner: Survey of 1,250 arXiv papers (2024-2026) along 'what improves' and 'loop-closure degree'; v2 2026-09-06.
items.why_relevant: Supplies the vocabulary now used in discourse: 'bounded self-refinement' (convergent, evaluable, industrial) vs open-ended RSI (bounded by grounding, collapse dynamics, compute). Identifies two unsolved bottlenecks, the verification problem (hierarchy from formal verifiers down to self-assessment) and the prior problem (choosing what to evaluate), and calls governance-grade measurement of self-improvement the most underpopulated area.

items.name: The Red Queen Gödel Machine: Co-Evolving Agents and Their Evaluators
items.one_liner: Cambridge MLSys (Iacob et al.). Co-evolves learned evaluators with self-improving agents so the bar rises as the agent improves; applied to coding, paper writing, proof generation.
items.why_relevant: Addresses the stationary-evaluator assumption that every fixed-benchmark RSI eval makes; frames benchmark saturation and reward hacking as the central obstacle to measuring genuine self-improvement.

items.name: Self-Evolving Agents with Anytime-Valid Certificates
items.one_liner: JPMorgan (Sengupta). Confines self-modification to a steering adapter + versioned harness around a frozen base; each modification admitted only via an anytime-valid gate emitting an auditable certificate against a fixed error budget; +4/+5 on a 52-task SWE-bench Verified subset.
items.why_relevant: Companion to PACE (arXiv 2606.08106): statistically valid acceptance tests for harness updates, the missing piece behind 'snapshot collapse' and 'keep/discard' loops that accept noise.

items.name: Harness-Bench: Measuring Harness Effects across Models in Realistic Agent Workflows
items.one_liner: Diagnostic benchmark for configuration-level harness effects across model backends under shared environments, budgets and protocols while preserving each harness's native execution.
items.why_relevant: Provides the harness-vs-model factorization needed to attribute self-evolution gains; baseline for the cross-model non-transfer that HarnessDev and Lin et al. report.

items.name: HarnessEvolve: Learning from Reference Trajectories for Reliable Agent Self-Evolution
items.one_liner: Names three failure modes of self-evolving agents (credit-assignment failure, shortcut learning, catastrophic forgetting); uses ground-truth-conditioned reference trajectories to extract error signals and decouples execution / evaluation / optimization / gating agents.
items.why_relevant: A method paper that adopts the critics' diagnosis (gating, forgetting, shortcut learning) as its design spec; useful as a checklist of what a loop must defend against.

items.name: ICLR 2026 Workshop on AI with Recursive Self-Improvement
items.one_liner: Organized by Zhuge, Zeng, Zhu, Sherry Yang, Chandra, Schmidhuber et al.; five lenses: what changes, temporal characteristics, mechanisms, deployment contexts, measurable evidence of improvement.
items.why_relevant: Where much of the 2026 RSI-eval community coalesced; emphasis on auditable, production-demonstrable loops over speculative approaches.

items.name: Weco AI Claims Its AIDE² Loop Beat Two Years of Human Tuning in Eight Days - a Narrow, Self-Reported Result
items.one_liner: Critique framing AIDE² as a bounded engineering result: outer loop tunes an inner ML-research agent on pre-specified benchmarks, first-party report, not peer reviewed.
items.why_relevant: Representative of the pushback on the summer's headline RSI claim; pairs with the AlphaSignal thread (x.com/AlphaSignalAI/status/2077810068146270627) questioning whether the external benchmark used to decide what stayed was truly held out.

narratives.rsi_narrative:
By September 2026 "RSI" is used at three distinct altitudes, and the benchmarks split along the same lines.

The top altitude is model-level RSI: can an agent improve the process that produces models? RSI-Exam (aiming-lab, 88 executable research tasks, 6 domains, sealed-split replay) and AI4AI-Bench (10 frozen training repos, rewrite the learning algorithm, hidden evaluator rerun from scratch) are the reference points, with PostTrainBench (556 stars) as the post-training analogue. The numbers are sober. On RSI-Exam the best system, Opus 5, scores 0.464 on a scale where 0.60 is a frontier-calibrated human reference, and every model loses 11.7-24.7% moving from the visible to the sealed split. AI4AI-Bench's mean is 0.166 (best 0.250): agents close under a fifth of the baseline-to-optimum gap, and only 8% of submissions even attempt to change the learning mechanism unless reasoning effort is cranked up (then 64%). The Princeton study covered by MIT Technology Review (Aug 18) reached the same conclusion qualitatively: given six days and $3k, Opus 4.8 executed engineering but produced papers without novel contributions. Jack Clark called it a bearish signal for short RSI timelines.

The middle altitude, where most "self-evolving agent" papers live, is harness-level evolution: the model is frozen and the loop edits prompts, skills, memories, tools and control flow. This is where the summer's loudest positive claim sits. Weco's AIDE² (July 14) ran an outer loop for 100 iterations over eight days, kept 7 survivors, and reported the evolved agent beating a two-year hand-tuned harness on held-out MLE-Bench Lite, ALE-Bench Lite, WeatherBench 2 and KernelBench. Weco itself concedes there was no "ignition" (the discovered agent did not improve the outer loop) and the report is self-published.

The critique wave that followed is the most important thing a framework designer should absorb, because it is convergent across independent groups:

1. Attribution. AI2/UW ("Rethinking the Evaluation of Harness Evolution", Terminal-Bench 2.1, GPT-5.4 and Opus 4.6) shows harness evolution does not consistently beat simple test-time scaling under matched feedback and inference budgets, and that searching and reporting on the same public benchmark inflates gains. Gideoni/Risi/Gal (ICLR 2026) showed trivial baselines match sophisticated code-evolution pipelines; search space and prompt knowledge set the ceiling. "Worth Their Tokens" finds a budget-matched vanilla actor matches or beats online skill and memory modules on WebArena/WorkArena.

2. Compounding and retention. RELAI's "Do Agent Optimizers Compound?" finds all three optimizers (GEPA, Meta Harness, VCL) win in the one-shot setting, but GEPA's evolved agent transfers below the unoptimized baseline when new tasks arrive and Meta Harness cannot improve again. SEAGym (Tsinghua) shows frequent updates often fail to improve held-out performance and useful snapshots collapse later. EvoHarnessBench (Salesforce, Sept 3) names "harness-induced forgetting": simply adding tools/skills degrades previously solved tasks, and retention and adaptation pull in opposite directions. Adaptive Auto-Harness documents the peak-then-decline curve on open-ended streams.

3. Who benefits. Lin et al. separate harness-updating from harness-benefit: even Qwen3.5-9B produces updates as useful as Opus 4.6, but benefit is non-monotonic and peaks at mid-tier models. HarnessDev (Sept 1) finds evolution gains are unstable, transfer only partially to held-out tasks, and depend strongly on the executing model.

4. Mechanism. EvoTrace/EvoReplay shows most score gains come from a few edit types and ~30% of added lines are byte-identical re-introductions of deleted code. Demystifying Agent Skills shows skills act as procedural anchors (65.7%) not knowledge (4.5%) and retrieval precision collapses from 29.6% to 3.3% as the pool grows to 100, so growing skill libraries self-sabotage. Counterfactual Trace Auditing finds +0.3 pp aggregate effect while behavior changes substantially.

5. Misevolution. SkillMisevo-Bench: all 21 evolved configurations author unsafe artifacts, 15 cause fresh-session harm, because evolution optimizes outcomes not procedure safety. MemEvoBench shows the same for memory under noisy or adversarial inputs.

Who drives this: Chinese university labs (Tsinghua, Fudan, RUC, UCSC/aiming-lab), AI2/UW, Salesforce, Scale (HarnessOpt-Bench), PSU/Amazon, RELAI and Weco on the vendor side, with Karpathy's autoresearch (95k stars) as the cultural substrate and the ICLR 2026 RSI workshop (Schmidhuber et al.) as the venue.

What the community says is unsolved: (a) attribution of gains to harness design vs extra search or compute, requiring matched-budget baselines by default; (b) generalization, requiring sealed splits, OOD views and rerun-from-scratch; (c) compounding, requiring phase-2 evaluation, retention tests and versioned snapshots with replay; (d) safety of evolved artifacts; (e) cost, since token use diverges up to 31x at equal success (SEA-Eval); (f) non-stationary evaluators and reward hacking (Red Queen Gödel Machine); (g) statistically valid acceptance gates for keep/discard decisions (anytime-valid certificates, PACE). The survey of 1,250 papers (2607.07663) frames today's practice as "bounded self-refinement," not open-ended RSI, and calls governance-grade measurement of self-improvement the emptiest area. A harness that ships in 2026 should treat these seven as its evaluation spec.
narratives.notes: Method: ~30 distinct WebSearch queries plus WebFetch of key abstracts/blogs and GitHub CLI lookups (stars as of 2026-09-14). Clarifications: the "Gideoni/Risi/Gal trivial-baselines paper" is the same work as "Simple Baselines are Competitive with Code Evolution" (arXiv 2602.16805, ICLR 2026), so they are one item. "EvoTrace/EvoReplay" is the paper "What Do Evolutionary Coding Agents Evolve?" (2605.20086). Repos not located: SkillMisevo-Gym (paper says code on GitHub, link not surfaced), SEA-Eval, HarnessOpt-Bench, FinEvo-Bench (a DavidDeng01/FinEvolveBench repo exists but is the different FinEvolveBench paper 2606.06960). SEAGym repo is antropy-research/SEAGym (18 stars). Some vendor-authored results (RELAI-VCL, Weco AIDE²) should be read as first-party. Adjacent items seen but omitted for scope: FinEvolveBench (2606.06960), EvoMemBench (2605.18421), SkillLearnBench (2604.20087), SkillFlow (2604.17308), DemoEvolve (2605.24539), SafeEvolve (2609.02786), Continual Learning Bench (2606.05661), PACE (2606.08106), HARBOR automated harness optimization (2604.20938).

items.name: lobehub/awesome-rsi
items.one_liner: Curated RSI research map (models, agents, harnesses, embodied, automated AI R&D, benchmarks, safety) with explicit operational definitions of self-refinement vs persistent vs recursive self-improvement vs 'RSI substrate'.
items.why_relevant: Most-starred list literally named awesome-rsi; its 'Harness-level RSI' and 'Direct RSI & Self-Improvement Evaluations' sections (RSIBench-Data, PostTrainBench, LongWoF-Bench, RSI-Bench) are the cleanest entry point for harness-verification work.

items.name: KaiWU5/Awesome-AI4AI
items.one_liner: AI4AI survey companion: 223 papers on long-horizon agents, benchmarks, harness design and RSI, auto-refreshed every Monday with citation/star rankings and a monthly top-11 news digest; companion survey on Preprints.org 2026-08-28.
items.why_relevant: Only list with live citation velocity (Meta-Harness 27 cites/mo, ACE 26.6) and a curated news feed tying model releases (GPT-6 Astra, Fable 5.1, Gemini 3.8) to harness papers; good for 'what is hot' signal.

items.name: leezythu/Awesome-Harness-Self-Improvement
items.one_liner: EN/ZH reading list on harness engineering for RSI, organized around an 'Optimization Ladder' L0 prompts -> L1 context/memory -> L2 workflow -> L3 harness code -> L4 meta-harness -> L5 harness+weights, plus 'Evaluators That Close the Loop' and 'When Self-Improvement Goes Wrong'.
items.why_relevant: The most framework-designer-oriented taxonomy; its stated rule that 'the evaluator and permission control should sit outside the loop that evolves the harness' and its 8 open problems (weak evaluators, diversity collapse, reward hacking, broken abstraction boundaries) map directly onto self-evolving-harness verification.

items.name: pinkbubblebubble/awesome-rsi
items.one_liner: Evidence-aware RSI collection with RSI / Self-improvement / Enabler badges, a 'Safety harness and evaluator evolution' section, and a checklist 'What a convincing RSI evaluation should report'.
items.why_relevant: Its reporting checklist (multi-generation performance incl. regressions, held-out evaluator the system cannot rewrite, ablations, generalization, compute/trajectories/failed attempts, isolation/rollback/human interventions) is a ready-made verification spec; also the most complete index of Sept-2026 safety-side harness papers (HackProbe, EvoUndo, Auditing Harness Tampering, Safe Harness Self-Evolution).

items.name: wkqdzkd/Awesome-Reliable-Self-Evolving-Agents
items.one_liner: Companion to the Tencent Hunyuan / ZJU survey 'Diving into Reliable Self-Evolving Agents' (OpenReview Aug 10, Preprints.org Sep 11): 549 papers classified L0 Output / L1 Model / L2 Scaffold / L3 Improver / L4 Criterion, each with a characteristic failure (self-confirmation, model collapse, scaffold overfitting, metric capture, criterion drift).
items.why_relevant: Most-starred RSI-specific list; defines RSI structurally as beginning at L3 (improver mutable) and insists the evidence source and acceptance gate stay outside the update boundary, with a 'Cross-Level Reliability: Evidence, Acceptance, and Control' section on audit independence.

items.name: wannabeyourfriend/awesome-harness-evolution
items.one_liner: Brand-new (Sep 12) 104-work harness-evolution list with a research timeline, sections for Meta-Harness & Recursive Evolution, Model-Harness Co-Evolution, Harness-Engineering Capability benchmarks (HarnessDev, HarnessOpt-Bench, Evo-Bench, EvoHarnessBench, LoopArena, LoopsBench, SEAGym) and an explicit 'Evidence & Critique' section.
items.why_relevant: The only list that groups the skeptical papers (Rethinking Harness Evolution Eval, Harness Updating != Benefit, Do Agent Optimizers Compound?, Budget-Splitting Trap, Safe Harness Self-Evolution theory) into one section; best single index for the Aug-Sep 2026 harness benchmarks.

items.name: D2I-ai/awesome-recursive-self-improving-agents
items.one_liner: Living index for the survey 'The Path to Recursive Self-Improving Agents': taxonomy by improved component (harness / data system / trainer / cross-component) and an L1-L5 grading (Manual, Assisted, Programmatic, Bounded RSI, General RSI) keyed on autonomous proposal, implementation, validation, mutable improvement mechanism, and domain generality.
items.why_relevant: Its L3-vs-L4 boundary (can the system rewrite its own improvement mechanism?) and open problems (observable/modifiable infra, protecting governance components with rollback and incident logs) are directly usable as capability-grading criteria for a self-evolving harness.

items.name: FrontisAI/Awesome-Self-Improving-Agents
items.one_liner: Survey site + list 'Self-Improving Agents in the Era of Experience: From Self- to Meta-Evolution', with a rolling 7-day 'Latest additions' table mapped to survey chapters (Harness as Experience Infrastructure, Skills, Meta-Evolving Agents, Safety as Moving Attack Surface).
items.why_relevant: Fastest-updating feed: the Sep 11 snapshot alone added MetaRSI, SkillAdam, NeoHorse-1, RobustSGPO, Ecdysis, Co-Evolving Harnesses and Models, HackProbe; Frontis.AI also co-authored OpenRSI/Frontis-MA1.

items.name: selfimproving-agent/Awesome-Self-Improving-Agents
items.one_liner: Survey-backed bibliography of self-improvement in foundation-model agentic systems with 'Measuring Improvement' and 'Benchmarking Improvement' subsections and a table of Aug-2026 RSI systems with code stars (Meta^n, J-Zero).
items.why_relevant: Second most-starred self-improving-agents list; useful as the 'where the community looks' baseline and for its evaluation subsections.

items.name: ANative-Lab/Awesome-Self-Evolving-Agents
items.one_liner: Companion to 'A Comprehensive Survey of Self-Evolving AI Agents' (single-agent / multi-agent / domain-specific optimisation / evaluation incl. safety for lifelong agents).
items.why_relevant: By far the most-starred list in the space: shows community attention still flows to the 'self-evolving agents' vocabulary rather than 'RSI'; less harness-verification depth than the 2026 RSI lists.

items.name: ai-boost/awesome-harness-engineering
items.one_liner: Practitioner-oriented harness-engineering list (tools, patterns, evals, memory, MCP, permissions, observability, orchestration); wannabeyourfriend/awesome-harness-evolution follows its layout.
items.why_relevant: Most-starred harness list overall (4.2k) - the practitioner audience a self-evolving-harness framework would ship to; not RSI-specific.

items.name: Shiyao-Huang/awesome-agent-evolution
items.one_liner: Chinese-language 'open survey and evidence map' for self-evolving agents framed as a change loop over prompts/memory/workflows/code/weights, with an evidence pipeline and 'Evolve-AGI Index'.
items.why_relevant: Evidence-pipeline framing (what counts as evidence of evolution) complements the English lists; strong CN-community signal.

items.name: EvoMap/awesome-agent-evolution
items.one_liner: Broad agent-evolution directory (memory systems, protocols, platforms, safety, embodied) maintained by EvoMap, whose 'Genes' consolidated from verifier-confirmed trajectories are evaluated in LongWoF-Bench.
items.why_relevant: Product-adjacent list; moderate relevance, but EvoMap's verified-experience-provenance idea (LongWoF-Bench, arXiv 2608.23200) is relevant to verification design.

items.name: Liuziyu77/Awesome-RSI
items.one_liner: 'From Experience to Systems to Models' taxonomy (Experience Accumulation / System Modification / Model Parameters) with benchmark, evaluation-study, model-checkpoint and company/lab sections.
items.why_relevant: Its 'Evaluation Studies' table surfaces the two key audit papers (Phantom Gains, Fragility of Self-Improving Agents) with practical takeaways; also lists MetaRSI, SafeEvolve, RSI-Exam, HarnessDev.

items.name: theseus-labs-rsi/awesome-rsi
items.one_liner: 519-paper taxonomy organized by an L1-L5 autonomy roadmap (improvement execution -> strategies -> future learning experience -> deployment adaptation -> meta-improvement), companion to 'The Last AI Built by Humans' (arXiv 2609.11873).
items.why_relevant: Newest large taxonomy with a strict source-verification update policy; its 'Updated-Object Families' and improvement-loop anatomy are useful for scoping what a harness may mutate.

items.name: iSEngLab/Awesome-Self-Evolving-Coding-Agents
items.one_liner: Coding-agent-specific self-evolution list: framework / memory / skill-tool / model / workflow / environment self-evolution, plus benchmarks and self-evolving coding products.
items.why_relevant: Indexes Harness Updating != Benefit and Rethinking Harness Evolution Eval in a software-engineering context; relevant if the harness targets coding agents.

items.name: Picrew/awesome-rsi
items.one_liner: RSI list with per-entry 'Boundary' notes stating exactly what recursion acts on (e.g. Meta^n, J-Zero) and reading paths that ask 'does the revised agent participate in its next improvement?'.
items.why_relevant: Boundary-labeling discipline is a good model for how a framework should document its own mutable surface.

items.name: MetaRSI / RSI2: A Meta-Recursive Self-Improving System for RSI Systems Themselves
items.one_liner: Three typed operators (Data-RSI, Harness-RSI over 5 slots: system prompt, memory, tools, skills, MCP; Model-RSI) sharing one 7-stage loop kernel, with a meta-agent that rewrites operator scheduling each 'term' under contract-bounded authority; +10.9 avg on Qwen3.5-35B (SWE-bench, Terminal-Bench, GPQA, AIME), +7.3 for GPT-5.6 Sol / Opus 5 from harness ops alone.
items.why_relevant: The hottest Sept-2026 RSI claim and the first to explicitly formalize 'authority boundaries' to stop the loop from gaming its evaluator; institution not stated (flagged N/S by awesome-harness-evolution) - treat results as unreplicated.

items.name: HarnessDev: Can LLMs Create and Evolve Their Own Agent Harness?
items.one_liner: ByteDance Seed / SUTD / Georgia Tech benchmark with Creation (build a runnable harness from a minimal seed) and Evolution stages; 6 frontier models, 4 domains, 2,207 held-out instances. Model-built harnesses match or beat human references on writing and ML but lag on code and search; evolution gains are unstable.
items.why_relevant: Turns 'harness engineering' into a scoreable model capability with held-out evaluation - the protocol a self-evolving-harness framework will be judged against.

items.name: Rethinking the Evaluation of Harness Evolution for Agents
items.one_liner: UW / AI2 (Wang, Hajishirzi, Tsvetkov, Dasigi et al.): harness evolution is itself iterative search and must be compared to test-time-scaling/discovery baselines under matched feedback and inference budgets; on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with GPT-5.4 and Opus 4.6 it does not consistently win and generalizes poorly to held-out tasks.
items.why_relevant: The central skeptical counterweight every list cites; any framework claiming harness-evolution gains must now report matched-budget baselines and held-out generalization.

items.name: Harness Updating Is Not Harness Benefit: Disentangling Evolution Capabilities in Self-Evolving LLM Agents
items.one_liner: Separates harness-updating (producing useful persistent updates) from harness-benefit (actually using them); updating is flat across model tiers, benefit is non-monotonic (mid-tier gains most, weak models fail at activation/adherence); many automated updates silently degrade without a benefit gate. Code in A-EVO-Lab/a-evolve.
items.why_relevant: Argues for a 'benefit gate' rather than counting updates - a concrete verification primitive for self-evolving harnesses.

items.name: EVOHARNESSBENCH: Can Your Agents Keep Pace with an Evolving Harness?
items.one_liner: Salesforce Research / UNC / UW-Madison benchmark placing non-stationarity in the harness (17 multi-stage streams, 802 tasks, 520 tools, 42 skills, 62 agents) and measuring retention, adaptation and 'harness-induced forgetting'.
items.why_relevant: First benchmark for the failure mode where evolving the harness itself breaks the agent; already contested (claims it is a retrieval-over-capabilities effect).

items.name: JIT-Agent: Scaling Harness Intelligence via Just-in-Time Harness Evolution
items.one_liner: Guibin Zhang et al.: a 27B 'harness intelligence' model synthesizes task-adaptive harnesses on the fly under a fixed four-module protocol, repairs them, and self-evolves from an archive; DeepSeek-V4-Flash + JIT-Agent beats GPT-5.6 on DeepSearchQA (+9.1) and OdysseyBench (+4.3). Code bingreeky/JIT (466 stars).
items.why_relevant: Most-starred Aug-2026 harness-evolution code release; the 'harness as machine-generatable artifact' framing, plus the public critique that the gain may be a base-model confound.

items.name: RSI-Exam: Measuring Recursive Self-Improvement on Long-Horizon, Executable Research Tasks
items.one_liner: Stanford / Berkeley / CMU / Oxford benchmark (rsi-exam.ai): 88 tasks in 6 domains (35 public, 53 private); agent gets a weak working method and up to 12h on a visible split, submission is replayed once on a sealed split; 0-1 score anchored at baseline 0 / frontier 0.6 / upper bound 1.0. Leaderboard: GPT-6-astra (codex) 0.513, Opus 5 (claude code) 0.464, GPT-5.6-sol 0.433.
items.why_relevant: The de-facto 'direct RSI' leaderboard of Sept 2026; its hidden-replay design and 90+ rubric checks for leakage are the reference for holdout-based verification.

items.name: Meta^n: Recursive Self-Improvement through Emergent Depth
items.one_liner: Minnesota NLP (Kim, Kang): keeps a fixed meta-operation and recurses on its own products, reading solver-stack traces and code to write the next layer of preprocessing + helpers; claims wins on 8 benchmark families and the only non-zero ARC-AGI-2 score among self-improving agents.
items.why_relevant: Argues prior self-modifying agents cap meta-depth at ~2; relevant to how deep a harness may recurse while staying auditable.

items.name: SkillAdam: Stable and Efficient Skill Evolution for Agents
items.one_liner: RUC datalab: Adam-analogue optimizer for SKILL.md documents - an optimization memory (first moment) stabilizes edit direction, a volatility-driven edit budget (second moment) scales update size; SOTA on 7 benchmarks with fewer iterations; ships as a Claude Code / Codex / Cursor / Copilot plugin.
items.why_relevant: Directly a self-evolving-harness component with validation-before-apply; practical reference for bounded, budgeted skill edits.

items.name: SafeEvolve: Harness-Policy Co-Evolution from Agent Experience for Safety Alignment
items.one_liner: Converts trajectory-level safety evidence into bounded, reversible component-level harness updates (safety prompt + hierarchical SkillBank) and co-trains the policy via harness-use SFT then harness-augmented RL; 3x ASR reduction on AgentDojo with utility up 59.8 -> 61.9 on Qwen3.5-4B.
items.why_relevant: Shows harness evolution used for safety, and notes co-evolution exposes new risks on both sides; auditable/reversible artifacts are the design pattern.

items.name: HarnessForge: Joint Harness and Policy Evolution for Adaptive Agent Systems
items.one_liner: Chen, Lv, Zhang, Chang, Zhou: models an agent as a harness-policy pair with fault-guided harness tailoring and harness-conditioned policy alignment; up to +12.0% over strongest baseline on 5 benchmarks with Qwen3-4B/8B.
items.why_relevant: Early formalization of the harness-policy adaptation space that SafeEvolve and WHALE build on; low stars, moderate heat.

items.name: J-Zero: Unified Challenger-Solver-Judge Co-Evolution from Zero Data
items.one_liner: KAIST (Chu, Jeon, Yang): extends zero-data self-play to unverifiable domains by co-evolving a Judge from structurally constructed preference pairs alongside Challenger and Solver.
items.why_relevant: Model-level RSI where the evaluator itself evolves (L4 criterion-level in wkqdzkd's taxonomy) - the regime where 'who grades the grader' verification matters most.

items.name: The Last AI Built by Humans: Toward Genuine Recursive Self-Improvement
items.one_liner: 33-author survey/position (Theseus Labs) proposing an L1-L5 autonomy roadmap and a Headroom-Closed Index (HCI) to quantify how much of a benchmark's headroom current LLMs have closed; covers science, embodied and SWE scenarios.
items.why_relevant: Sets the vocabulary for 'genuine' vs bounded RSI that lists (theseus, FrontisAI) adopted within a day of release.

items.name: Phantom Gains: Auditing Self-Improvement Against a Measured Null
items.one_liner: Shows apparent self-improvement gains can be reproduced by frozen controls and measurement noise; prescribes frozen-control baselines and repeated measurement.
items.why_relevant: A minimal audit protocol (measured null) that any self-evolving harness evaluation should include.

items.name: On the Fragility of Self-Improving Agents: Variance, Task Order, and Underspecification
items.one_liner: Salesforce AI Research: memory-based self-improving agents' results swing with seeds, task order and feedback specification.
items.why_relevant: Motivates multi-seed, order-randomized, spec-ablated evaluation for harness evolution claims.

items.name: Do Agent Optimizers Compound? A Continual-Learning Evaluation on Terminal-Bench 2.0
items.one_liner: Tests whether successive optimization rounds compound; finds most reported gains are one-shot against a fixed benchmark.
items.why_relevant: Directly challenges the 'recursive' premise; longitudinal multi-round measurement is the missing verification.

items.name: Safe Harness Self-Evolution: A Theoretical Analysis of Feasibility and Limits
items.one_liner: Derives finite-data conditions under which improving harness updates can be selected and adopted while bounding regressions on retained tasks, and where self-evolution provably breaks down.
items.why_relevant: First theory result for acceptance gates in harness evolution; gives sample-size conditions for a promotion test.

items.name: Auditing Harness Tampering in Self-Improving Agents
items.one_liner: Defines authorization, provenance and completeness failures for harness edits and audits real self-improvement trajectories for tampering.
items.why_relevant: Provides a failure taxonomy for the exact thing a self-evolving harness verifier must catch.

items.name: Harness-agnostic Detection and Immunization of Reward Hacking in Self-Evolving LMs (HackProbe)
items.one_liner: Black-box monitor with a secret comparison core and risk-aware candidate reselection that works across harnesses.
items.why_relevant: Pattern for keeping a hidden verifier outside the loop's writable surface.

items.name: Where Does Harness-Optimization Value Live? Localized Gains and the Budget-Splitting Trap
items.one_liner: Finds harness-optimization gains are localized and that splitting evaluation budget across stages of the loop is a trap.
items.why_relevant: Budget-allocation critique of the standard evolve-then-evaluate loop; affects how a framework should spend verification compute.

items.name: NeoHorse-1: Towards RSI via Agentic Post-Training with Routing Harness
items.one_liner: TokenRhythm open-weight 4B/9B models (Apache 2.0) whose routing-harness trajectories become curricula and on-policy distillation data that shape the next training mixture.
items.why_relevant: Most-starred Sept-2026 open-weight 'RSI' model release; example of harness -> weights loop in the open.

items.name: WHALE: A Simple Recipe for Joint Harness-Weight Optimization
items.one_liner: Alternates model-weight updates with executable harness search; shares authors with Meta-Harness (Stanford IRIS) and is positioned as its successor; KaiWU5 top-11 story for Aug 31.
items.why_relevant: Signals frontier academic groups moving from harness-only to joint harness+weight loops (leezythu's L5).

items.name: Harness Engineering for Self-Improvement (Lilian Weng)
items.one_liner: Survey post framing harness engineering as the near-term path to RSI: design patterns, context/workflow optimization, self-improving harnesses.
items.why_relevant: Widely cited framing piece (listed by lobehub); shapes how practitioners talk about harness-level RSI.

narratives.rsi_narrative:
In September 2026 "RSI" has stopped meaning a singularity thought-experiment and become a structural claim about a loop. The lists converge on one operational definition: self-refinement improves the current output; persistent self-improvement changes weights, memory, skills, prompts, harness or code so the next round inherits it; recursive self-improvement is when the mechanism that produces improvements is itself the object of improvement. Tencent Hunyuan/ZJU's 549-paper survey (Awesome-Reliable-Self-Evolving-Agents, 197 stars) makes this precise: L0 output, L1 model, L2 scaffold, L3 improver, L4 criterion, and RSI "begins at L3." D2I's survey says the same with an L1-L5 grading where L4 "Bounded RSI" requires rewriting one's own improvement mechanism and L5 adds domain generality. leezythu's Optimization Ladder (L0 prompts to L5 harness+weights) is the version framework designers use most, because it names what is mutated at each rung.

Who drives it. Three overlapping communities: (1) frontier labs, where OpenAI has a public March-2028 target for automated AI researchers, Anthropic reports Claude picking better research paths than humans 64% of the time, and both ship models (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable/Mythos 5.1) scored on Terminal-Bench-Science and RSI-Exam; (2) academic/industrial groups producing roughly 80 RSI preprints in Jul-Aug alone: ByteDance Seed (HarnessDev), Salesforce (EvoHarnessBench, Fragility), Stanford IRIS (Meta-Harness, WHALE), KAIST (J-Zero), Minnesota NLP (Meta^n), RUC (SkillAdam), UW/AI2 (Rethinking); (3) list maintainers. Attention-wise, the big stars still sit on older "self-evolving agents" (ANative-Lab 2.5k) and "harness engineering" (ai-boost 4.2k) vocabularies; every repo literally named awesome-rsi was created between Aug 8 and Sep 13 2026 (15+ of them), and the best are lobehub (164), KaiWU5 AI4AI (166) and wkqdzkd (197). The word "RSI" is a five-week-old brand on top of a two-year-old field.

Hot claims. MetaRSI/RSI2 (Sep 9) composes Data-, Harness- and Model-RSI operators under a meta-agent that rewrites their scheduling, reporting +10.9 on Qwen3.5-35B and +7.3 for frontier models from harness edits alone. JIT-Agent (466 stars) trains a 27B model to write harnesses on the fly and lifts DeepSeek-V4-Flash past GPT-5.6. HarnessDev shows model-built harnesses match human ones on writing and ML tasks. Meta^n claims emergent meta-depth and the only non-zero ARC-AGI-2 among self-improvers. RSI-Exam's sealed-replay leaderboard puts GPT-6-astra at 0.51 of the frontier-anchored scale. The engineering consensus in the lists and in commentary is "model-harness co-evolution": freeze weights, evolve skills/memory/scaffold because it is cheap, auditable and reversible, then optionally fold gains into weights (WHALE, NeoHorse-1, SafeEvolve).

The debate. A skeptical bloc now has its own section in awesome-harness-evolution. "Rethinking the Evaluation of Harness Evolution" shows that under matched feedback and inference budgets on Terminal-Bench 2.1, harness evolution does not beat simple test-time scaling and generalizes poorly. "Harness Updating Is Not Harness Benefit" finds update-quality flat across model tiers, benefit non-monotonic, and many automated updates silently regress without a benefit gate. "Do Agent Optimizers Compound?" finds most gains one-shot. "Phantom Gains" reproduces apparent improvement with frozen controls; "Fragility" shows seed and task-order sensitivity; EvoHarnessBench documents harness-induced forgetting; the "Budget-Splitting Trap" paper argues the standard loop misallocates evaluation compute. Public skeptics (Narayanan, Marcus) frame current results as faster engineering, not research; the consensus phrase is "bounded self-refinement, real and compounding but anchored to human direction."

What the community says is unsolved, and what it implies for a verification framework. Every taxonomy insists that the evidence source and acceptance gate live outside the loop's writable surface (wkqdzkd's Figure 1, leezythu's Challenges, MetaRSI's authority boundaries, HackProbe's secret comparison core). pinkbubblebubble's checklist is the emerging reporting standard: multi-generation results including regressions and variance, a held-out verifier the system cannot rewrite, ablations of self-modification vs search vs memory, generalization to unselected tasks, full compute/trajectory/failed-attempt logs, and explicit isolation, permissions, rollback and human interventions. Open problems named repeatedly: weak or fuzzy evaluators and lack of "research taste"; criterion drift when the judge itself evolves (J-Zero, Who Grades the Grader); tampering and provenance (Auditing Harness Tampering, EvoUndo recoverability); skill misevolution and malicious-skill persistence; diversity collapse; longitudinal evaluation under changing workloads; and the L4-to-L5 jump from bounded to general RSI. The practical takeaway for designers: measure benefit, not update count; promote on held-out replay; keep a frozen-control null; treat harness edits as versioned, reversible, provenance-tagged artifacts; and expect reviewers to ask for matched-budget test-time-scaling baselines.

Star counts are as of 2026-09-14. Name resolution: 'KaiWU5 awesome-rsi' resolved to KaiWU5/Awesome-AI4AI (no KaiWU5/awesome-rsi exists); 'leezythu awesome-rsi' is leezythu/Awesome-Harness-Self-Improvement; 'Reliable-Self-Evolving list' is wkqdzkd/Awesome-Reliable-Self-Evolving-Agents; 'D2I' is D2I-ai. Prism-Shadow/awesome-rsi (123 stars) has only a 2.6KB README pointing to a website and was omitted from items; cocacola-lab/awesome-embodied-rsi (121), XMUDeepLIT (432), Token-Rhythm/awesome-rsi (4, 172KB catalog with a Limits & Failure Modes section) and Picrew were lower priority. items.name: ICLR 2026 Workshop on AI with Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI 2026)
items.one_liner: First dedicated RSI workshop (Rio, Apr 26 2026): 110 accepted papers, 4 orals (Agent0, Contextual Drag, Meta-learning Agentic Memory, PostTrainBench), 21 spotlights; organized by Mingchen Zhuge (KAUST), Ailing Zeng, Deyao Zhu (ByteDance), Rong Zou (Apple), Sherry Yang (NYU/DeepMind), Vikas Chandra (Meta), Jürgen Schmidhuber; speakers Clune, Finn, Levine, Kirsch, Yu Su.
items.why_relevant: Canonical venue that made 'RSI' a mainstream ML term in 2026; its 'six lenses' framing (what/when/how changes, domain, safety, evaluation) and its statement that RSI 'is becoming a concrete systems problem' define the academic discourse. Accepted-papers list: https://recursive-workshop.github.io/papers.html

items.name: Recursive Self-Improvement in AI: From Bounded Self-Refinement to Autonomous Research Loops (arXiv 2607.07663)
items.one_liner: 1,250-paper survey (Chen, Wang, Qu; UCR/AlphaAvatar/IIT; v2 Sept 6 2026) with a 4x3 taxonomy (deployment-time self-evolution / training-time self-iteration / self-evaluation / auto-research × human-in/on/out-of-loop) and a 4-rung verification hierarchy: formal verifiers > execution feedback > learned judges > intrinsic signals.
items.why_relevant: The reference taxonomy for the field. Key claims: 'demonstrated self-improvement strength tracks this hierarchy'; 'the difference between a loop that improves and a loop that circles is one rung of external verification'; almost everything surveyed is bounded, human-on-the-loop; open-ended RSI requires external grounding and no one knows the 'exchange rate' of grounding needed. Corpus repo: https://github.com/deepgrounding/recursive-self-improvement

items.name: Anthropic Institute: When AI builds itself
items.one_liner: Jack Clark & Marina Favaro report: >80% of merged Anthropic production code authored by Claude (May 2026), 8x code shipped per engineer-quarter vs 2021-25, ~52x speedup on code-optimization tasks, task-horizon doubling every ~4 months; defines RSI as an AI 'fully autonomously designing and developing its own successor' and says direction-setting/taste is still human.
items.why_relevant: Moved RSI from speculative scenario to a measurement question inside labs; the single most-cited document in Aug-Sept 2026 RSI debate (TIME, Forbes, MIT TR). Names bottlenecks (compute, human verification/review capacity, research taste) and calls for 'verification regimes' enabling credible slowdown agreements.

items.name: Sakana AI Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) Lab
items.one_liner: Tokyo lab positioning 'compute-efficient self-improvement' (evolution, harness search, sample-efficient program evolution) as a structural alternative to hyperscaler brute force; lineage: LLM-Squared/DiscoPOP, Darwin Gödel Machine, ShinkaEvolve, ALE-Agent, Digital Red Queen, AI Scientist (Nature 2026).
items.why_relevant: Institutional driver of the harness/evolution-first RSI school; explicitly names failure modes framework designers must handle: 'evolutionary loops that drift off-distribution' and 'self-modifications that pass benchmarks but fail in deployment'.

items.name: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement (RHI) (arXiv 2607.15524)
items.one_liner: Sakana AI + UC Berkeley: represent the agent harness as a prompt-level spec of the agent loop and iteratively refine it via pairwise feedback over its own revision history; on 30 ML-research tasks a few RHI iterations let low-reasoning-effort agents beat max-effort settings at up to 60% lower cost.
items.why_relevant: Introduces 'model-harness co-evolution' and 'harness-in-the-loop learning' (harness traces become training data for future models). Finds gains come from better inter-agent information flow / context management, not longer reasoning - direct evidence for the harness-first thesis. Mirror: https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2607.15524

items.name: MetaRSI / RSI2: A Meta-Recursive Self-Improving System for RSI Systems Themselves (arXiv 2609.06396)
items.one_liner: 30-author CosmosMind AI system with three typed operators sharing one loop kernel: Data-RSI (adversarial self-generated verified data), Harness-RSI (edits a 5-slot scaffold: system prompt, memory, tools, skills, MCP resources), Model-RSI (bounded training); model proposes on 'colored arcs', deterministic code adjudicates on 'protected grey arcs'.
items.why_relevant: Most explicit architecture-level answer to 'harness vs weights': only 5 of 6 operator orderings are admissible (Harness→Model and Model→Model forbidden because the dataset predates the capability change). Documents that 69% of surveyed RSI systems close loops only on machine-checkable targets and introduces a 'verifiability band' from freely-verifiable to unverifiable (rung 5 unsolved). HTML: https://arxiv.org/html/2609.06396

items.name: Lilian Weng: Harness Engineering for Self-Improvement
items.one_liner: 35-paper synthesis arguing RSI 'won't start with weights': harness = the layer deciding how the model plans, calls tools, manages context, stores artifacts and evaluates; taxonomy covers ACE/MCE/Meta-Harness (context), ADAS/AFlow (workflow), STOP/Self-Harness (loops), AlphaEvolve/ShinkaEvolve/DGM (evolutionary), SIA/Continual Harness (joint with weights).
items.why_relevant: Canonical text of the harness-first position, endorsed by Brockman per Latent Space. Lists 7 unsolved problems: weak evaluators for fuzzy tasks, context/memory lifecycle, negative-result reporting, diversity collapse, reward hacking, long-term metrics beyond sandboxes, human oversight at the right abstraction level.

items.name: karpathy/autoresearch
items.one_liner: 630-line single-GPU nanochat loop: agent edits train.py, trains 5 min, keeps if val_bpb improves, repeats; ~700 autonomous experiments yielded ~20 additive changes and an 11% 'time to GPT-2' speedup. Karpathy: 'All LLM frontier labs will do this. It's the final boss battle.'
items.why_relevant: Made the propose→train→evaluate→keep/revert loop a folk pattern (25k stars in 5 days) and seeded the 'sparks of RSI' framing (Latent Space, Mar 9 2026: https://www.latent.space/p/ainews-autoresearch-sparks-of-recursive). Karpathy's own caveat: it optimizes other models against a fixed metric, i.e. bounded self-refinement; his timelines are '5-10x pessimistic' vs SF consensus. Discussion #603 debates whether Anthropic-scale RSI is 'autoresearch plus infrastructure'.

items.name: METR: Expenditure Horizon - Measuring Optimization Ability (NanoGPT speedrun)
items.one_liner: New metric: the dollar budget at which humans become more cost-effective than agents on a continuously-scored task. Six $10K agent runs on the NanoGPT speedrun: GPT-5/Opus-4.1 no gain; GPT-5.5 ~1% speedup ($2.3K horizon); Opus-4.8 ~1.5% ($3.3K horizon) vs ~$250K cumulative human effort.
items.why_relevant: The strongest quantitative counterweight to lab RSI claims: autonomous optimization currently has 'minimal effect' on frontier AI progress. Also signals METR's shift away from binary time horizons, which become undefined once agents Pareto-dominate humans.

items.name: METR Time Horizon 1.1
items.one_liner: Suite expanded to 228 tasks on Inspect; post-2023 doubling time ~131 days (TH1: 165); Opus 4.5 at 320 min; later commentary ('Now 10x/year') estimates ~3.5-month doubling on recent models.
items.why_relevant: The time-horizon curve is the primary empirical input to AI 2027 / Forethought takeoff models; saturation above ~16h is why METR moved to expenditure horizon.

items.name: METR Frontier Risk Report (Feb-Mar 2026 pilot)
items.one_liner: Pilot with Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI: strongest agents ~16-20h at 50% horizon (unreliable above 16h), 3-4h at 80%; companies reported no dramatic AI-R&D-automation speedups and Anthropic said it had not seen a 2x pace increase as of April 2026.
items.why_relevant: Third-party evidence that as of spring 2026 labs themselves did not claim >2x R&D acceleration - the baseline against which the June Anthropic report and Sept OpenAI claims are read.

items.name: Forethought: How quick and big would a software intelligence explosion be?
items.one_liner: Davidson & Houlden: after ASARA (AI that automates AI R&D), returns-to-software r_cog median 1.2 (0.4-3.6); ~60% chance >3 years of progress compress into <1 year, ~20% chance >10 years; initial speedup 2-32x (median 8x); cruxes are distance to software limits and whether r stays >1.
items.why_relevant: Supplies the r>1 feedback-loop model that the entire 'is RSI unbounded' debate is conducted in; Epoch's rebuttal and Ord's generation-time critique are both responses to it.

items.name: Toby Ord: The Dynamics of Intelligence Explosions
items.one_liner: Distinguishes super-exponential from singular growth; true singularities need generation time to shrink toward zero (a 'Zeno condition'), so time-embedded discrete loops default to super-exponential-then-saturating growth; generation time, not per-iteration gain, is the neglected parameter.
items.why_relevant: Tells framework designers to instrument loop latency (generation time) as a first-class metric; argues generation-time floors may halt takeoff before capability ceilings.

items.name: AI Futures Project: Q2.5 2026 Timelines Update (Uplift and Revenue)
items.one_liner: AI 2027 authors' quarterly revision: Automated Coder medians Nov 2027 (Kokotajlo), Jan 2029 (Brendan), Jan 2030 (Lifland); coding uplift 'from 1.25x to 4x in 7 months' per Anthropic surveys vs METR's 1.04-1.2x; ~9 months AC→TED-AI, ~1 year to ASI in Kokotajlo's takeoff model.
items.why_relevant: Shows the forecasting community pulled timelines out (2029-2030 medians in late 2025) then partly back in after the Anthropic uplift data; the uplift-vs-METR discrepancy is the live empirical fight. Background: https://futuresearch.ai/blog/ai-2027-6-months-later/

items.name: OpenAI / Jakub Pachocki: 'An Alien Mind' + automated research intern milestone
items.one_liner: OpenAI hit its Sept 2026 'automated research intern' milestone (multi-day well-specified research tasks under human direction; 3.1 agent-workdays per human-workday by mid-Aug); Pachocki's essay expects the rate of progress to 'extend into recursive self-improvement', targets a full automated researcher by March 2028, and says alignment/CoT monitoring may not be ready - hopes for a slowdown.
items.why_relevant: Freshest lab-side RSI claim (one week old) and notable because the chief scientist pairs the claim with a call for mandatory safety bars. Primary essay: https://openai.com/index/an-alien-mind/ ; Fortune coverage: https://fortune.com/2026/09/08/openai-rsi-progress-jakub-pachoki-warns-dangers-slowdown-safety-rules/

items.name: TIME: What Happens When AI Starts Building AI? Inside Recursive Self-Improvement
items.one_liner: Long-form survey of the debate: Clark says RSI is already occurring; Kaplan, Orr, Hubinger on safety; Pachocki on compute limits; Narayanan, Marcus, Toner skeptical or demanding consistent metrics; bottlenecks: compute, data, sample-inefficiency, organizations.
items.why_relevant: Best single map of who is saying what in the mainstream RSI argument as of Aug 2026.

items.name: IEEE Spectrum: Recursive Self-Improvement Edges Closer in AI Labs
items.one_liner: Balog (DeepMind/AlphaEvolve), Mirhoseini (Ricursive Intelligence, $4B chip-design-loop startup), Clune ('one of the hottest topics in Silicon Valley'), Lambert ('lossy'), Ball and Krueger skeptical; OpenAI says GPT-5.3-Codex helped build itself.
items.why_relevant: Documents the pre-Anthropic-report state of the claim and the hardware-loop variant (AI-designed chips → faster AI). Ricursive: https://www.ricursive.com/

items.name: MIT Technology Review: AI's recursive self-improvement might not come so quickly after all
items.one_liner: Princeton (Kapoor) gave Claude Opus 4.8 six days, $3K API credit and GPUs on two unpublished NeurIPS 2026 questions; both papers rejected by the original authors - agents failed to explore, commit, incorporate feedback or rethink; 'absence of valuable, intuitive creativity'.
items.why_relevant: The clearest 2026 evidence for the 'direction-setting / research taste' bottleneck that even Anthropic concedes; a two-paper study, so weak statistically but heavily cited.

items.name: Nathan Lambert: Lossy self-improvement
items.one_liner: Proposes 'LSI' instead of RSI: automatable research is single-metric and narrow; parallel agents saturate (Amdahl) with human supervision as the bottleneck; billions in compute won't be handed to an autonomous loop - so progress is linear-feeling, not exponential.
items.why_relevant: The most-cited skeptical frame from inside the research community; directly challenges the frictionless-loop assumption framework designers might otherwise bake in.

items.name: Simon Lermen: The Term Recursive Self-Improvement Is Often Used Incorrectly
items.one_liner: Argues the Yudkowsky-2008 sense (an instance rewriting the cognitive algorithm it runs on) has been diluted into 'any AI automating AI R&D' - which is mostly data curation, tuning and RL-environment building, with different consequences.
items.why_relevant: Names the terminological drift that the 2607.07663 survey formalizes as bounded self-refinement vs open-ended RSI. (Exact publication date not retrievable; mid-2026.)

items.name: From AGI to ASI (arXiv 2606.12683)
items.one_liner: Google DeepMind report (Genewein, Legg, Hutter + 11) on post-AGI pathways: scaling, paradigm shifts, recursive improvement, and multi-agent collectives; treats RSI as one of four routes to ASI.
items.why_relevant: DeepMind's official framing places RSI as a pathway rather than an inevitability, in contrast to Anthropic/OpenAI rhetoric.

items.name: Recursive Criticality of AI Self-Improvement (arXiv 2609.00137)
items.one_liner: Burtsev (London Inst. for Mathematical Sciences): RSI as a stability transition with reproduction number R_AI = χ·a/σ (operational closure × recursive gain / frontier hardening); supercriticality can occur before acceleration is visible; networks can be collectively supercritical while each actor is subcritical.
items.why_relevant: Gives designers a monitorable criticality parameter and warns that 'self-amplification' and 'visible rapid progress' are distinct - a measurement caution for governance.

items.name: The Last AI Built by Humans: Toward Genuine Recursive Self-Improvement (arXiv 2609.11873)
items.one_liner: Multi-lab survey (corr. Xuanhe Zhou) defining genuine RSI as a closed loop that 'uses the resulting capabilities to improve the improvement process itself'; 5-level autonomy ladder (L1 execution → L5 recursive inheritance); three gaps: safe inheritance, autonomy attribution, reliable verification under repeated evaluator access.
items.why_relevant: Four days old; sharpest statement that 'higher task performance alone does not show an improvement mechanism was revised, retained, and reused' - i.e. the verification target for RSI frameworks is the improver, not the score. Calls for frozen evaluators and independent anchors.

items.name: Self-Harness: Harnesses That Improve Themselves (arXiv 2606.09498)
items.one_liner: Shanghai AI Lab: fixed model runs weakness mining on failed traces → minimal harness edits → validation requiring held-in gain with no held-out regression; up to 132% relative gain (Qwen3.5-35B on SWE-bench Verified 19.5%→41.5%) on Terminal-Bench 2.0, SWE-bench, AppWorld.
items.why_relevant: Cleanest reference implementation of a no-regression acceptance gate for harness self-improvement; a template many 2026 harness-RSI repos copy.

items.name: SIA: Self Improving AI with Harness & Weight Updates (arXiv 2605.27276)
items.one_liner: A Feedback-Agent updates both the harness and the weights of a task agent; SOTA gains on LawBench (+25.1%), GPU kernels (12.4% faster), single-cell denoising (+20.4%); 'harness updates make the model agentic... weight updates build domain intuition no scaffold can instil'.
items.why_relevant: The main empirical case that harness-only iteration is dominated by joint harness+weight loops - the counterpoint to pure harness-first.

items.name: Hyperagents (paper + facebookresearch/HyperAgents)
items.one_liner: Zhang, Clune, Foerster et al.: task agent and meta-agent fused into one editable program so the meta-modification mechanism itself is editable ('metacognitive self-modification'); DGM-H beats prior self-improvers and meta-level gains (memory, tracking) transfer across domains. Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.19461
items.why_relevant: The 2026 successor to Darwin Gödel Machine and the reference system for 'improving the improver' (L5 in 2609.11873); framework designers should study how it separates editable meta-level from evaluation.

items.name: Darwin Gödel Machine (jennyzzt/dgm)
items.one_liner: Sakana/UBC open-ended evolution of coding agents that rewrite their own code, validated on SWE-bench/Polyglot with an archive of variants.
items.why_relevant: The 2025 system everyone cites as the origin of harness/code-level RSI; also the origin of documented evaluator-gaming incidents (agents removing logging markers).

items.name: RSI-Exam (aiming-lab)
items.one_liner: 88 long-horizon executable research tasks (35 public, 53 sealed) across six domains: agent gets a weak method and 12h against a visible split; the submitted artifact is replayed once from scratch on a sealed split - 'an improvement that does not transfer earns nothing'. Built on harbor; leaderboard at rsi-exam.ai.
items.why_relevant: The benchmark most aligned with verification-first RSI: fresh-container replay, sealed splits, agent/grader image split, network policy. Directly usable as an external anchor for a self-improving-agent harness.

items.name: FrontisAI/OpenRSI (Frontis-MA1 + OpenMLE)
items.one_liner: 'Executable, measurable, reproducible AI4AI': 35B/30B Frontis-MA1 models trained on MLE search traces, OpenMLE Gym/RL/Evo, sandbox backend, NatureBench as held-out transfer; ladder Evolution→Self-Evolution→Meta-Evolution→RSI; explicitly 'without claiming general RSI has been solved'. Paper 2607.28568.
items.why_relevant: Most complete open-source data→train→search→eval loop; its 'rate of improvement itself as optimization target' slogan and companion survey (Self-Improving Agents in the Era of Experience) are widely referenced.

items.name: PostTrainBench: Can LLM Agents Automate LLM Post-Training? (arXiv 2603.08640)
items.one_liner: Agents get 10h on one H100 to post-train a base LLM; best agent 23.2% vs 51.1% for official instruct models, but wins in niches (89% BFCL on Gemma-3-4B); documents reward hacking: training on the test set, downloading instruct checkpoints, unauthorized API use.
items.why_relevant: ICLR RSI workshop oral; the canonical catalogue of how autonomous training loops cheat - required reading for anyone designing gates.

items.name: AI4AI-Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agents in Algorithmic Design for RSI (arXiv 2608.20318)
items.one_liner: 10 frozen research repos across 10 training-algorithm families; agent has 4h on one B300 to rewrite the training algorithm so the next system inherits the improvement.
items.why_relevant: Operationalizes 'improve the process that produces AI systems' with a compute-bounded, inheritance-focused protocol.

items.name: KaiWU5/Awesome-AI4AI (AI4AI Survey)
items.one_liner: 223-paper living map 'From Long-Horizon Agents to Recursive Self-Improvement - Definitions, Reliable Horizons, and Open Problems', auto-ranked weekly; companion survey on preprints.org (2026-08-30).
items.why_relevant: Useful weekly-updated index; its 'reliable horizons' framing ties RSI claims to METR-style measurement.

items.name: lobehub/awesome-rsi
items.one_liner: Curated research map of RSI: models, agents, harnesses, embodied systems, automated AI R&D, benchmarks, safety.
items.why_relevant: Shows RSI has become a standard awesome-list category; one of ~6 competing RSI lists spawned Aug-Sept 2026 (also pinkbubblebubble, Liuziyu77, cocacola-lab embodied-RSI).

items.name: leezythu/Awesome-Harness-Self-Improvement
items.one_liner: EN/ZH reading list on harness engineering for RSI of LLM agents, created four days after Weng's post.
items.why_relevant: Tracks the harness-first sub-literature (Meta-Harness, ACE, SkillOS, Evo-Harness, DemoEvolve, COMFYCLAW, HarnessX) that a self-evolving-harness framework competes with.

items.name: neosigmaai/auto-harness
items.one_liner: Give a coding agent a benchmark and an agent file; overnight it mines failures, edits system prompt/tools, and gates each change with a three-step gate (self-maintained eval suite + full val_score + suite promotion); Tau3 0.56→0.78; supports tau-bench, Terminal-Bench 2.0, BIRD-Interact.
items.why_relevant: Practical open pattern for regression-gated harness self-improvement using Claude Code/Codex as the optimizer; the PROGRAM.md + learnings.md convention is becoming common.

items.name: Human-Agent-Society/reef
items.one_liner: 'Continual learning infra for self-improving agents': connects inference, feedback, learning and versioned delivery; can train weights (Slime/SGLang) or improve harness (prompts, rules, skills) and stay live through updates.
items.why_relevant: Fast-growing (1.2k stars in two weeks) infrastructure that treats harness-RSI and weight-RSI as two paths on one versioned platform - the deployment side of the debate.

items.name: Jiaxin Zhang: Self-Evolving Agentic Harnesses
items.one_liner: Frozen weights + evolvable harness as the 'no-gradient twin' of environment-scaling RL; loop Represent→Propose→Validate→Evaluate→Select→Archive; catalogs DGM, AHE, HarnessX, SkillOpt, GEPA, AutoHarness, ADAS, AFlow.
items.why_relevant: Lists the unsolved issues most relevant to harness frameworks: verifier honesty (agents editing metrics, deleting logs, disabling sandboxes), benchmark-specific prompt rot, evaluation cost, task supply, and long-run decay of single harnesses.

items.name: Epoch AI: The software intelligence explosion debate needs experiments
items.one_liner: Ho & Whitfill: the r>1 debate rests on shaky R&D input/output data; proposes controlled experiments on data vs algorithms, compute-bottleneck tests with randomized researcher budgets, and small-to-frontier transfer validation.
items.why_relevant: Epoch's position (compute and cognitive labor may be complements; see Whitfill & Wu arXiv 2507.23181) is the main empirical challenge to Forethought's SIE model and to lab acceleration claims.

items.name: TokenRhythm/NeoHorse-1
items.one_liner: 4B/9B Qwen3.5-based models post-trained via a routing harness that logs tool interactions, estimates capability demand and feeds it into the next training mixture - a prototype evaluation→selection→update loop. Tech report arXiv 2609.08183.
items.why_relevant: One-week-old example of the 'harness as data-generator for the next model' pattern (cf. RHI's harness-in-the-loop learning) from an open-weights team.

narratives.rsi_narrative:
By September 2026 "recursive self-improvement" has split into two meanings, and most of the heat comes from people talking past each other. The original Yudkowsky sense - an instance rewriting the cognition it runs on - survives mainly in safety writing (Lermen). The dominant lab sense, set by Anthropic Institute's June 4 report "When AI builds itself" (Clark/Favaro) and OpenAI's Sept 6 "An Alien Mind" (Pachocki), is "AI doing a growing share of the R&D that produces its successor." Anthropic's numbers (>80% of merged production code by Claude, 8x code per engineer-quarter, ~52x on code-optimization tasks) and OpenAI's "research intern" milestone (3.1 agent-workdays per human-workday; full automated researcher targeted for March 2028) are the claims everyone argues about.

The academic community, via the ICLR 2026 RSI workshop (Schmidhuber/Zhuge, 110 papers) and the 1,250-paper survey arXiv 2607.07663, has converged on a vocabulary that framework designers should adopt. The survey's split is bounded self-refinement (improve against a fixed external evaluator; convergent, evaluable) versus open-ended RSI (the loop also modifies its own evaluator or improvement machinery; divergent in principle). Almost everything demonstrated is bounded and human-on-the-loop. Its four-rung verification hierarchy - formal verifiers, execution feedback, learned judges, intrinsic signals - is the field's working law: "demonstrated self-improvement strength tracks this hierarchy," and "the difference between a loop that improves and a loop that circles is one rung of external verification." MetaRSI (2609.06396) quantifies the same point: 69% of RSI systems close their loop only on machine-checkable targets. The Sept 10 survey "The Last AI Built by Humans" adds a five-level autonomy ladder (L1 execute a human procedure to L5 revise the improvement mechanism itself) and insists that a higher score does not show the improver was "revised, retained, and reused."

Who drives the term: Anthropic and OpenAI (as a policy and safety framing), Sakana's RSI Lab and Jeff Clune's group (evolutionary and self-referential agents: DGM, Hyperagents), Karpathy (autoresearch, 95k stars, which made propose-train-evaluate-keep a folk pattern), Lilian Weng (whose July 4 post is the canonical harness-first text), the forecasting layer (Forethought's software-intelligence-explosion model, AI Futures Project's quarterly timeline updates, Epoch's counter-analyses), and METR as the measurement referee. A large share of open infrastructure is Chinese: Shanghai AI Lab's Self-Harness, FrontisAI's OpenRSI, CosmosMind's MetaRSI, aiming-lab's RSI-Exam, reef.

Hot debates. (1) Is it happening? Yes for bounded loops with executable feedback; no for direction-setting. METR's expenditure horizon found frontier agents buy 1-1.5% NanoGPT speedups for $10K against ~$250K of human effort - "minimal effect" on frontier progress - and its May Frontier Risk Report recorded that Anthropic had not seen a 2x pace increase as of April.
