deep_reads.name: Harness Engineering for Self-Improvement (Lilian Weng, Lil'Log)
deep_reads.last_activity: 2026-07-04 (published; page carries no dateModified metadata, so no later edits detected). Companion community reading list leezythu/Awesome-Harness-Self-Improvement last pushed 2026-09-08.
deep_reads.org_or_authors: Lilian Weng (Thinking Machines Lab co-founder; formerly OpenAI Head of Safety Systems). Single-author survey/position post.
deep_reads.venue_or_citations: Lil'Log (lilianweng.github.io), 31-min read. Reception: author's X announcement ~405K views (per AINews 2026-07-08 lead story 'Lilian Weng summarizes 35 papers on Harness Engineering for RSI'); Hacker News 334 points / 80 comments; endorsed publicly by Sakana AI (ties it to AI Scientist and DGM) and, per a KuCoin news headline I could not fetch directly, by DeepSeek's Cui Tianyi; spawned a bilingual community reading list (88 stars, 5 forks, created 4 days after the post). A commenter noted the survey omits Gödel Machine (2003), GPTSwarm (2024) and Agent-as-a-Judge (2024). No academic citation count applies; Weng's posts are habitually cited in papers.
deep_reads.mechanism: Survey/position post (6,643 words, 39 references, 17 figures), not a system; it ships no code and runs no experiments. Defines a harness as "the system surrounding a base model that orchestrates execution and decides how the model thinks and plans, calls tools and acts, perceives and manages context, stores artifacts, and evaluates results," and argues near-term RSI will start by optimizing this layer rather than weights. Part 1 gives three design patterns: a plan-execute-test-improve workflow loop (Karpathy autoresearch as exemplar); the file system as persistent memory so state outlives the context window; explicit, inspectable sub-agents and backend jobs whose outputs land in files, not chat. Part 2 orders the literature by the object optimized, along the progression "instruction prompts -> structured context -> workflow -> harness code -> optimizer code": (a) context engineering: ACE (generator/reflector/curator over itemized bullets merged deterministically), MCE (bi-level: outer loop evolves context-management skills, inner loop optimizes the context; both run as coding agents with Read/Write/Edit/Bash/Glob/Grep/TodoWrite), Meta-Harness (coding agent proposes harness code; each candidate is a directory of source, scores and traces; keeps a Pareto frontier of accuracy vs context cost); (b) workflow: AI Scientist, ScientistOne (chain-of-evidence audit), Autodata (challenger / weak solver / strong solver / verifier), ADAS (meta-agent programs agents in code, archive-on-success), AFlow (MCTS over workflow graphs); (c) self-improving harness: STOP (improver improves itself via meta-utility), Lin et al. (harness-updating vs harness-benefit), Self-Harness (weakness mining -> bounded proposal -> validate on held-in and held-out), AHE (7 file-level components; runs/tracer/verifier/LLM config read-only; every edit is a falsifiable predicted-impact manifest); (d) evolutionary: Promptbreeder, GEPA, AlphaEvolve (edits confined to EVOLVE-BLOCK regions), ShinkaEvolve (embedding-based novelty rejection), DGM/Hyperagents (agent edits its own repo; pool keeps high performers); (e) joint with weights: SIA (feedback agent routes between harness and weight updates), Continual Harness. Part 3 lists six observed auto-research failure modes and seven bottlenecks, concluding that "the evaluator and permission control should likely sit outside the loop that evolves harness, with held-out tests, trace audits, and human review at decision points that matter."
deep_reads.eval_loop: The post runs no evaluation of its own; it reports the loops of surveyed systems, all of which use benchmark pass-rate as fitness plus a keep/discard rule: ADAS archives candidates that score well; AFlow adds a workflow to the MCTS tree only if it improves within N rounds and stops when top-k plateaus; STOP scores an improver by mean downstream utility over a task set; Self-Harness accepts an edit only with no regression on held-in D_in and held-out D_out (the paper additionally requires strict improvement on at least one split); AHE keeps the verifier, tracer, runs directory and LLM config read-only and pairs every edit with a predicted-impact manifest checked next round; DGM adds agents to the pool only above a performance bar and samples parents by score and inverse child count; ShinkaEvolve rejects candidates too similar to the population; Meta-Harness keeps a Pareto set on accuracy vs context tokens. Benchmarks cited: Terminal-Bench-2, SWE-bench Verified, Polyglot, plus an appendix of research-agent benchmarks (PaperBench 8,316 rubrics; CORE-Bench 270 tasks; ScienceAgentBench 102 tasks; RE-Bench 7 envs with 71 human 8-hour attempts; MLE-bench 75 Kaggle competitions; KernelBench 250 tasks, fast_p metric).
deep_reads.key_results: Numbers quoted in the post (all from cited papers, none original): DGM with Claude 3.5 Sonnet lifts SWE-bench Verified 20.0% -> 50.0% and Polyglot 14.2% -> 30.7% (matches the DGM paper). STOP improves mean downstream utility with GPT-4 but degrades with GPT-3.5 and Mixtral. Lin et al.: harness-updating ability is roughly flat from Qwen3.5-9B to Claude Opus 4.6, while harness-benefit is non-monotonic with mid-tier models gaining most (paper adds: weak models load skills as little as 25% of the time vs 96%, and follow them 14% vs 75%). Self-Harness improves held-out pass rates for MiniMax M2.5, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B and GLM-5 on Terminal-Bench-2 (paper: M2.5 42.2% -> 53.9%; Qwen3.5-35B-A3B 18.0% -> 36.7%). AHE beats OpenCode, Terminus-2 and Codex on Terminal-Bench-2 except the Hard tier (paper: 77.0% vs Codex-CLI 71.9%, seed 69.7%, ACE ~74.6%, TF-GRPO ~74.2% with GPT-5.4; repo README now claims 84.7% with GPT-5.5). Meta-Harness numbers are shown only as a figure; the paper reports Terminal-Bench-2 76.4% (Opus) / 37.6% (Haiku) and text classification 48.6% vs ACE 40.9% at 4x fewer context tokens. Appendix baselines: PaperBench best ~21%; MLE-bench bronze-or-better in 16.9% of competitions; RE-Bench agents 4x humans at 2h but humans win at 8h and 32h.
deep_reads.safety_measures: As a survey it implements nothing; it catalogs and endorses: bounded editable surfaces (AlphaEvolve EVOLVE-BLOCK markers; Self-Harness 'editable surfaces'; AHE limiting edits to the harness workspace with runs directory, tracer, verifier and LLM configuration read-only, explicitly to block disabling the verifier, swapping the model or raising the reasoning budget); held-in plus held-out regression tests before merge; evidence-bound edits with falsifiable predicted-impact manifests; trace audits; permission controls and security layers living outside the self-modification loop ("if a program is allowed to edit the OS system, abstraction boundaries are broken"); and humans moving "up the stack" to oversight at decision points. It flags reward hacking against unit tests, judge models and benchmark artifacts, diversity collapse, over-optimism ("numerical duct tape"), and that sandbox RLVR ignores maintainability, ownership boundaries, migration cost and backward compatibility.
deep_reads.limitations: 1) Pure synthesis: no new method, code, or experiments; every number is second-hand and mostly from unreviewed 2026 arXiv preprints (25 of 39 refs are arXiv; 17 are dated 2026). 2) Editorial defects: refs [25] Yuksekgonul and [26] Riaz are listed but never cited in the body; the Lin et al. model range reads 'Qwen3.5-9B to Opus 4.6' in prose but 'Qwen2-32B to Opus 4.6' in the figure caption. 3) Selective reporting on the papers most relevant to acceptance: the post does not mention that AHE's falsifiable-manifest mechanism achieves only 11.8% precision / 11.1% recall at predicting regressions (33.7% / 51.4% for fixes) and that its 'transfer' to SWE-bench Verified is +0.4pp (75.6% vs 75.2% seed); its paraphrase of the Self-Harness gate drops the requirement of strict improvement on at least one split. 4) Treats evaluation and permission control as harness components in the definition, then argues they should sit outside the loop, without resolving the tension or specifying an interface. 5) Coverage gaps noted by readers: Gödel Machine (2003), GPTSwarm, Agent-as-a-Judge; also same-week follow-ups HASE (2607.03935, co-evolves weights and validator code) and Adaptive Auto-Harness (2606.01770, open-ended task streams with a Verifier gate and git harness tree). 6) HN critiques target the field it summarizes: no agreed fitness function for code quality ('vibes'), maintainability vs test-passing, heterogeneous tasks resisting comparable metrics, and one report that stripping prompts/skills/MCPs improved results. 7) Predictions ('harness improvements will be internalized into core model behavior') are unfalsifiable as stated.
deep_reads.key_insight: Every self-improving-harness system Weng surveys already contains an ad-hoc acceptance gate (archive-on-success, no-regression on held-in/held-out, Pareto-keep, novelty rejection, falsifiable predicted-impact manifests) and her own conclusion is that the evaluator and permission control must live outside the loop that evolves the harness; but the one paper she cites that tried to make edits self-verifying (AHE) predicts its own regressions with 11.8% precision, which the post omits, so the gate cannot be delegated to the proposer.
open_gaps: No interface or contract is proposed for the 'outside the loop' evaluator; the post names held-out tests, trace audits and human review but never specifies what a harness-agnostic acceptance boundary would consume or emit.
How much oversight can be scaled or automated is explicitly left open ('remains an open research area').

Acceptance is per consumer model, not per proposer: Lin et al. show a 9B model writes edits isomorphic to Opus but mid-tier models benefit most, so a gate must re-validate a harness against each model that will run it; no surveyed system does this.

Regression prediction is weak (AHE 11.8% precision) and the surveyed gates are single-benchmark pass-rate deltas; nothing measures long-term repo health, ownership boundaries, migration cost or backward compatibility, which the post itself names as unmeasured.
Diversity collapse and reward hacking are listed as bottlenecks with no candidate mechanism beyond ShinkaEvolve's embedding-novelty filter.
Negative results and rejected candidates are logged in Self-Harness but no surveyed system feeds rejection evidence back as a first-class training or audit artifact.

Evaluator co-evolution (HASE, Autodata's verifier, ACE's reflector) is not addressed: if the evaluator is inside the editable surface, the 'outside the loop' principle is violated; the post does not say which components must be frozen.
Transfer of accepted harnesses across models and benchmarks is asserted (AHE to SWE-bench) but the effect is +0.4pp; whether acceptance decisions generalize is untested.
Compute cost of acceptance (held-out re-runs per candidate) is never quantified in the post or most surveyed papers.
The post predates and does not cover HASE (2607.03935) and Adaptive Auto-Harness (2606.01770), which add whitelisted evaluator repair and a git 'harness tree' with a Verifier agent respectively.
deep_reads.relevance_to_acceptance_layer: Directly on-thesis: the post's own bottom line ("the evaluator and permission control should likely sit outside the loop that evolves harness, with held-out tests, trace audits, and human review at decision points") is an argument for factoring acceptance into a separate layer, and its definition of harness treats 'evaluates results' and 'permission controls' as harness responsibilities, which is exactly the coupling a harness-agnostic acceptance layer would break. What to reuse: (1) the file-system contract that recurs across Meta-Harness, MCE, AHE and DGM (a candidate harness = a directory containing source, scores, rollout traces, state) is a natural harness-agnostic input format for an acceptance gate, since every system already materializes candidates that way; (2) AHE's read-only set (runs directory, tracer, verifier, LLM config) is a concrete list of what the acceptance layer must own and the proposer must not touch, motivated by named attacks (disable verifier, swap model, raise reasoning budget); (3) the Self-Harness rule (accept only with Δ_in ≥ 0 and Δ_out ≥ 0, strict improvement on at least one; rejected candidates logged without touching the active harness) is the cleanest existing gate and is harness-agnostic in form; (4) AHE's manifest schema (evidence, root cause, fix, predicted fixes, predicted regressions) as a required attachment to every candidate, so the gate can score calibration of the proposer over time; (5) Meta-Harness's Pareto-keep (accuracy vs context cost) as a multi-objective acceptance criterion; (6) ShinkaEvolve's novelty rejection as a diversity guard. What it proves or supports: STOP's degradation with weaker models and Lin et al.'s flat-updating / non-monotonic-benefit result together show that net-negative 'improvements' are common and consumer-model-dependent, so an acceptance layer must evaluate a candidate against the model that will run it, not trust the proposer's strength. The 7 file-level components in AHE and the progression prompts->context->workflow->harness code->optimizer code give a scope taxonomy for what the gate must be able to diff and validate. What it disproves or cautions: self-verification by the proposer is not enough (AHE's 11.8% regression-prediction precision), pass-rate deltas on one benchmark are gameable and ignore long-term health, and the post shows 'transfer' claims can rest on sub-1pp effects. What it leaves open: no interface spec, no treatment of evaluator co-evolution (HASE, Autodata) inside the editable surface, no cost model for held-out re-validation, no mechanism to keep the gate itself from being optimized against, and no metric beyond benchmark pass rate for the maintainability and compatibility properties it says matter.

deep_reads.mechanism:
A 27B meta-model (Qwen3.6-27B fine-tune) writes a task-specific agent harness at inference time for a frozen executor LLM. The harness is a fixed four-module protocol h=(M,P,A,F): memory.py (BaseMemory: initialize/build_context/update), planning.py (BasePlanning: init_plan/should_replan/get_directive), action.py (BaseAction.run owns the think-act-observe loop via a RuntimeContext), tool_policy.py (BaseToolPolicy.select_tools decides which tools/skills are exposed per step) plus prompt.yaml (required keys system_prompt/planning/summary/final_answer/step). Input: task, protocol, tool registry, and reference material (descriptions of 11 seed harnesses, ~13k tokens, or 3 random full-source seeds). Output: five tagged code blocks installed into an isolated workspace and imported by a shared kernel (AgentRuntime) — same path for hand-written seeds.

Training (paper): Stage I SFT on teacher-generated valid harnesses + DPO where a harness is preferred only if reward improves, neither latency nor cost degrades, and one efficiency axis strictly improves. Stage II repair SFT: failed harnesses paired with structured diagnostics (compile errors, interface mismatches, tool-call failures, runtime exceptions), teacher patches ≤2 rounds, keep trajectories that become executable. Stage III Evo-GDPO: sample G candidates, compare to the bank incumbent (highest reward, ties → lower latency, then cost); three decoupled reward channels R_rew=r+λ[r−b_r]+, R_lat=1[r≥b_r][b_l−l]+, R_cost=1[r≥b_r][b_κ−κ]+, each group-normalized, combined with w_rew>w_lat+w_cost; PPO+KL; bank retains a candidate only if it matches/exceeds the reward frontier and strictly improves ≥1 dimension.

Inference (repo): generate N=3 at T=1.0 → static gate (all 5 blocks emitted) → select by teacher-forced self-log-prob or LLM judge → execute on the benchmark item → on exception only, regenerate from scratch up to 5 times; low score never triggers repair. Optional (off by default, fail-open) 5-expert review panel fed a compile()/YAML static report. Streaming mode: bank retrieval per task, generator frozen.
deep_reads.eval_loop: 9 benchmarks in 4 families: deep research (BrowseComp-Plus acc, DeepSearchQA F1, xBench-DeepSearch acc), daily work (AgentIF-OneDay rubric, PinchBench), planning (DeepPlanning-Shopping cart match, DeepPlanning-Travel constraint score), workspace (OfficeBench, OdysseyBench success). Executors: GLM-5.2, DeepSeek-V4-Flash (main), Qwen3.6 and Mimo-V2.5 families (Fig. 4). Baselines: frontier models (GPT-5.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro/3.5 Flash, Kimi K2.7) and fixed harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Hermes, NanoBot) on the same executor. Repo pipeline: generate/select/execute artifacts, resume-idempotent, retries only infrastructure failures. Judge model defaults to deepseek-v4-flash (same as default executor). Fixed-seed baselines run with rollouts=1, max_repairs=0 while JIT runs best-of-3 with up to 5 crash-regenerations. Streaming test-time evolution (Fig. 6) reported on DP-Shopping, DP-Travel, OfficeBench as cumulative accuracy vs. static mode, no numbers in text.
deep_reads.key_results: Table 2 (BrowseComp+/DeepSearchQA/xBench/AgentIF/PinchBench/DP-Shop/DP-Travel/OfficeBench/Odyssey): GPT-5.6 76.9/76.0/81.0/68.0/84.2/83.7/84.9/65.3/68.7. GLM-5.2 base 72.0/89.2/76.0/63.0/87.0/78.2/62.8/63.0/75.3 → +JIT 78.0/93.9/88.0/69.9/93.3/83.4/83.0/68.4/78.7 (avg +7.7; largest +20.2 on DP-Travel). DeepSeek-V4-Flash base 68.1/76.2/70.1/58.4/81.7/59.1/54.8/61.0/71.0 → +JIT 74.0/85.1/82.0/63.8/92.9/83.9/61.3/63.4/73.0 (avg +8.8; +24.8 DP-Shop). DS-Flash+JIT beats GPT-5.6 on DeepSearchQA (85.1 vs 76.0, +9.1) and OdysseyBench (73.0 vs 68.7, +4.3) but trails it on 6/9. Table 3 controlled (DS-Flash executor; DeepSearchQA/xBench/AgentIF score @ $/task): Claude Code 79.6/75.0/66.9 @ .088/.079/.114; NanoBot 80.4/78.0/53.1 @ .131/.075/.147; OpenCode 75.9/65.0/48.1 @ .258/.159/.135; JIT 85.1/82.0/63.8 @ .066/.039/.097 — JIT wins search tasks at ~50% lower cost but loses to Claude Code on AgentIF. Fig. 4: six DeepSeek/Qwen/Mimo backbones avg +7.6 (DeepSeek +10.2, Qwen +4.0, Mimo +8.6). Avg 36% cost reduction vs fixed harnesses. deep_reads.limitations: No ablations of Stages I/II/III, repair, seed bank, N, or selector; no harness generation-failure or repair-success rates; teacher model, training compute, and task counts unstated in paper; no Limitations section. Base-model rows use an unspecified scaffold and GPT-5.6 is never run under a JIT harness, so the headline is confounded (raised in jjakimoto/research-issues #1433). Only Table 3 is controlled and covers 3 benchmarks x 2 executors. Test-time compute asymmetry: JIT gets best-of-3 plus up to 5 crash-regenerations; seed baselines get 1 rollout, 0 repairs; unclear whether meta-model/selector cost is in the $/task. Training tasks "come from existing agentic benchmarks" with no stated exclusion of eval sets; streaming bank risks cross-task leakage. Released checkpoint is Stage-I + distillation, not the Stage-III Evo-GDPO model; repo has no training code, no bank-update/retrieval code, and 11 seeds vs the paper's 13 (ReAct, AOrchestra missing), so 'harnesses keep improving at test time' is not reproducible. Judge and executor default to the same model. In the code, 'validation' is the scored run on the actual test item; library defaults (repair_only_on_error=False) would feed benchmark score/reason into repair — an oracle loop the CLI disables but does not remove. Review panel is off by default and fail-open; static check is only compile()+YAML keys; no interface-conformance check before execution; isolation is a workspace dir plus a 1h timeout, no sandbox or capability policy. Harness-agnostic only within its own kernel (issue #2 on OpenCode integration unanswered).
deep_reads.key_insight: Fixing a small typed protocol (4 ABCs + prompt schema + one shared kernel/install path) turns the harness into a verifiable, generatable artifact, and a strict Pareto-frontier acceptance rule (no regression on reward, strict gain on reward/latency/cost) can serve simultaneously as the preference signal, the RL bonus, and the archive-admission gate.
open_gaps: No quantitative reliability data: generation-failure rate, repair success rate, and how often the 5-repair budget is exhausted are never reported
Acceptance gates (static check, review panel, execution validation, frontier retention) are never ablated, so their contribution vs. raw best-of-N is unknown
All gating depends on a benchmark ground-truth evaluator; no story for accepting harnesses on tasks without a reward signal
Generated tool_policy.py controls the agent's own capability surface with no policy or safety check on what tools it exposes
Validation is single-item on the target task, not a regression suite across a distribution; archive hygiene and cross-task leakage in streaming mode are unmeasured
Released checkpoint and repo omit Stage III / bank evolution; the evolutionary claims cannot be reproduced
Confounded headline: same JIT harness never run on GPT-5.6; base rows' scaffold unspecified
Cost accounting excludes or does not state meta-model generation and selection overhead
Harness-agnosticism is untested outside the authors' own kernel (no Claude Code / OpenCode plugin path)
deep_reads.relevance_to_acceptance_layer: Directly relevant as a worked example of gating machine-generated harness code before it is allowed to run. Reusable pieces: (1) the contract-first design — a small fixed protocol (BaseMemory/BasePlanning/BaseAction/BaseToolPolicy, typed dataclasses, required prompt keys) plus a single install path where generated and hand-written harnesses are copied into an isolated workspace and imported identically; an acceptance layer should own exactly this surface so it can stay harness-agnostic. (2) A layered gate: deterministic static report (compile + schema keys) → LLM review panel of single-charter experts (action loop, tool invocation, termination, prompt parse, architecture proportionality) that receives the static report as ground truth, any-fail → regenerate with a bounded retry budget → bounded execution with structured diagnostics (compile/interface/tool-call/runtime) → repair only on execution error, never on low score (an explicit anti-Goodhart rule worth copying), with invalid-after-repair candidates receiving minimum reward while their latency/cost still count. (3) A concrete acceptance predicate for self-modification: admit only if primary reward matches/exceeds the incumbent and at least one of reward/latency/cost strictly improves, with incumbent tie-breaks reward → latency → cost; the same predicate builds DPO pairs, so the gate doubles as the training signal. (4) The runner's distinction between infrastructure failures (retried) and harness failures (counted) is a useful taxonomy for acceptance logs. What it proves: a 27B model can emit protocol-conformant executable harness code at scale, and per-task synthesis can beat fixed harnesses under a matched executor. What it does not prove: that any of the gates matter (no ablation, no failure-rate data), that the frontier rule resists leakage in a growing archive, or that the pattern transfers outside their kernel. What it leaves open for an acceptance layer: interface-conformance checks before execution (they only compile()), sandboxing and capability policy for generated tool_policy code, regression evaluation across a task distribution instead of the target item, verification without a ground-truth evaluator, cost accounting for the meta/verifier overhead, and keeping oracle score feedback out of the repair loop by construction rather than by CLI default. Negative lesson: their review gate is disabled by default and fail-open — an acceptance layer must be fail-closed and on by default to be meaningful.
deep_reads.safety_measures: Fixed protocol constrains generated code to four module interfaces; workspace isolation (copy five files into a per-unit directory, removed after run); execution budgets (max_steps 40, model_call_budget 3x steps, 1-hour validation timeout); optional 5-expert review panel gating on structural risks (dead ends, tool accessibility, termination, prompt parsing, over-engineering) — disabled by default and fail-open; repair triggered only by execution exceptions, never by low benchmark score (CLI default); invalid harnesses receive minimum reward; conservative frontier-only archive admission; KL penalty in PPO. No sandboxing of generated Python, no capability/tool-exposure policy, no safety evaluation, no discussion of misuse or of harnesses that alter their own tool surface.

deep_reads.name: RSI-Exam (aiming-lab) — Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement through Executable Research
deep_reads.mechanism: RSI-Exam is an evaluation harness (MIT, built on the harbor framework) plus a task bank of 88 "executable research" tasks in six domains (35 public on HuggingFace with full grading containers, 53 held back; full-suite eval by emailing the team). Each task ships two Docker images: an agent image containing a weak-but-working baseline under /app/methods/main/, visible data, and a selfcheck.py; and a separate verifier image (tests/) containing hidden data, trusted grade.py, and frozen anchors. The agent gets a fixed "autoresearch" prompt (LOOP FOREVER: hypothesise, build, measure with selfcheck, append to experiment_log.md, snapshot every version to methods/versions/vN including reverts, never delete), a 12h wall budget and 500k output-token budget reported by a mounted budget.py that reads each CLI's own logs (codex/claude/gemini/qwen/kimi) and prints wrap-up warnings at 90/95/99%. Network is no-network in both agent and verifier phases; the only opening is the model endpoint passed at run time via --allow-agent-host (SNI-matched allowlist; github/HF/zenodo/kaggle explicitly banned as label sources). Only the artifact (/app/methods) crosses into a fresh verifier container, which replays it once on the sealed split under a low-privilege sandbox (setuid nobody, RLIMIT_CPU/FSIZE/NOFILE/NPROC, JSON-over-stdin protocol, per-action timeouts, symlink/hardlink/size/TOCTOU checks, some tasks use bwrap). Raw metric is mapped through per-task anchors measured by the author: baseline→0, frontier-calibrated reference→0.6, upper bound→1 (piecewise-linear, or log interpolation with an exponential soft-cap for unbounded metrics; some tasks blend 0.7 anytime + 0.3 final). test.sh wraps the grader fail-closed: any exception, malformed output or disagreement among reward.txt/reward.json/score_details.json yields 0 with a "grader failed:" marker. Two artifact types: a method that solves the task directly, or a harness (prompt/memory/controller) driving a frozen model via an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Twelve model+harness combos are run, one rollout each, and the leaderboard is the mean hidden-set normalised score.
deep_reads.eval_loop: Inner loop (agent-side): selfcheck.py on visible split gives the only feedback; agent must log every version and snapshot; instructions tell it the visible score is a proxy and it must decide its own generalisation protocol (held-out slice, CV, repeats). Outer loop (benchmark-side): single sealed replay from scratch of the submitted /app/methods/main on hidden data in a separate no-network container; raw metric normalised against author-measured anchors (0/0.6/1); fail-closed to 0 on any invalid output, oversized file, missing entrypoint, timeout, or grader exception; the verifier also re-verifies artifact integrity (sha256 pins on anchors and scorer files in some tasks, e.g. bbo_noisy_continuous EXPECTED_ANCHORS_SHA256). Leaderboard = mean over 88 tasks, currently one rollout per model-task pair (harbor -k repeats supported but not used for the published board). Task acceptance pipeline: author writes task and runs baseline + a stronger reference end-to-end; developer builds the two-image format; reviewer 1 applies a 90+ item rubric (value, measurability, provenance/licensing, every lookup/memorisation leakage path); reviewer 2 audits a full agent trajectory against the anchors. Contribute page: "A number from a paper does not set the 0.60 mark; the method has to run on your data."
deep_reads.limitations: (1) No paper: the only write-ups are the blog and website; authorship is "RSI-Exam Team"; leaderboard rows have been added silently (GPT-6-astra 0.5126, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Qwen3.8-Max-0902 on Claude Code) after the blog/README, with no changelog. (2) Single rollout per model-task; tasks are stochastic; the team itself says repeats come in the next release, so rank differences of a few hundredths are not defensible. (3) Model and harness are confounded (same Qwen3.8 Max scores 0.3218 on qwen-coder vs 0.3923 on claude-code). (4) The 0.6 "frontier-calibrated reference" is not uniformly human SOTA: bbo_noisy_continuous's frozen_anchors.json records the frontier anchor as "codex gpt-5.6-sol sealed hidden run", i.e. one evaluated model's own rollout, which is circular for that model and makes 0.6 mean different things across tasks. (5) Normalisation curves differ per task (log vs linear vs anytime blends), so the mean is a mean of incommensurate scales. (6) Task quality bugs at release: gpus=1 stale config made lung_fewshot unrunnable on docker (fixed on HF); robotap verifier reportedly invokes the agent-side bwrap guard shim under rootless podman and scores the shipped baseline 0 (maintainers say Docker Engine works, left open); legal_matter task has filenames too long for some filesystems and aborts the whole hf download; grade.py in robotap swallowed exception text. (7) Four tasks depend on external pinned API models (gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4o, gemini-3-flash-preview) so anchors drift or break when those models change; verifier-side network hosts must be hard-coded in task.toml because harbor has no --allow-verifier-host. (8) Harness-side silent failures: antigravity-cli's 5-minute print timeout cut runs short and the half-finished work was graded with no error, requiring a patch script; gemini-cli silently substituted models. (9) "RSI" is a stretch: the scope statement concedes it measures bounded method/harness improvement, not weight modification or unrestricted self-improvement, and nothing measures whether improvements compound across tasks or rounds. (10) 53/88 tasks are private and evaluation on them is by email, so the headline numbers cannot be independently reproduced.
deep_reads.key_insight: Across every frontier model, gains the agent measured on the visible split shrank by 12-25% on the sealed replay (per-task it can be far worse: GPT-5.6-sol's DiscoveryWorld harness went 0.10→0.63 visible but only 0.13→0.26 hidden, normalised 0.27), so the acceptance signal that matters must be one the modifying agent cannot see and cannot run itself: a single from-scratch replay of the artifact in a fresh, network-sealed container, fail-closed to zero.
open_gaps: Only a terminal, one-shot acceptance: nothing gates individual changes mid-loop, and the agent never receives the hidden verdict, so there is no accept/reject feedback loop to study
No noise model: single rollouts, no confidence intervals, no stated minimum detectable improvement; an acceptance gate needs k-repeat variance to decide whether a delta is real
Anchors are heterogeneous and sometimes derived from a frontier model's own run (bbo_noisy_continuous), so 0.6 is not a stable cross-task reference
Per-task bespoke grade.py with different normalisation curves; no generic artifact contract or grader interface beyond harbor's reward.txt/reward.json convention
No cross-task or cross-round carryover, so the 'recursive' part (do improvements compound?) is unmeasured
Anti-gaming relies on sealing plus human leakage review; no automated detection of overfitting-to-visible, hard-coding, or test-set fingerprinting in the submitted artifact

Run-integrity of the agent phase is not verified by the verifier (antigravity 5-min truncation was graded as a normal run); model-actually-served and completion status are not first-class acceptance inputs
Verifier-side network policy cannot be set at run time (no --allow-verifier-host), which blocks LLM-judge style acceptance without editing the task
Reported task bugs (robotap verifier InfrastructureError under rootless podman, download failures) remain open; reproducibility outside Docker Engine unconfirmed
53 private tasks and the leaderboard are not independently reproducible; no paper, no per-run trajectories released for all models
deep_reads.relevance_to_acceptance_layer: Directly relevant as a reference design for the verification half of an acceptance layer, and as evidence for why one is needed. Reuse: (a) the two-image/one-boundary topology (agent container with visible data only; separate verifier container holding hidden data, trusted scorer and anchors; the artifact directory is the only thing that crosses) is harness-agnostic by construction, since harbor runs codex, claude-code, qwen-coder, antigravity, grok-build and kimi-cli with the same command differing in three flags; (b) the fail-closed grader wrapper (test.sh validating that reward.txt, reward.json and score_details.json agree, are finite, in [0,1], and that any exception collapses to 0 with a 'grader failed:' marker preserved) is a small, portable contract worth adopting verbatim; (c) the untrusted-artifact execution primitive (staged copy rejecting symlinks/hardlinks/non-.py files, TOCTOU stat check, setuid to nobody, rlimits on CPU/FSIZE/NOFILE/NPROC, JSON-over-stdin with per-action timeout and 64KB response cap, sha256 pins on scorer and anchors) is what a generic 'run the candidate' step should look like; (d) the anchored normalisation (baseline 0 / reference 0.6 / upper 1) converts heterogeneous metrics to one scale, which is what a cross-task acceptance threshold needs; (e) the mandated provenance trail (experiment_log.md with version id, parent id, change, scores, kept/reverted; every version snapshotted including reverts, never deleted) is an auditable lineage an acceptance layer can require and check; (f) network sealing rules (no-network in both phases, SNI allowlist supplied at run time, never widen to parent domains, banned label-source hosts) and least-privilege task-scoped API keys; (g) budget.py's harness-agnostic accounting by reading each CLI's own session logs. What it proves: sealed replay is necessary, not optional. All nine models in the blog lost 11.7-24.7% from visible to hidden on 37 comparable tasks; agents choose versions by visible score and overfit; harness-design tasks (agent improving the scaffold around a frozen model) are a measurable near-RSI target. What it disproves: that the agent's own generalisation discipline (told explicitly to hold out data and pick versions that transfer) is sufficient; it is not. What it leaves open: it is a one-shot terminal exam, not a per-change gate; there is no accept/reject feedback to the agent, no noise model (single rollouts), no compounding across rounds, anchors partly circular, per-task bespoke graders rather than a generic contract, no automated overfitting/hard-coding detection, and no verification that the agent phase itself ran as intended (the antigravity silent-truncation bug shows run-integrity metadata such as model-actually-served and completion status must be acceptance inputs). An acceptance layer for self-modifying agents would take RSI-Exam's verifier as the 'sealed replay' primitive and add: repeat-based statistical acceptance, per-iteration gating with the verdict fed back, artifact-diff and lineage checks against the logged versions, and run-integrity attestation.
deep_reads.safety_measures: Hidden data never enters the agent image; separate verifier container; no-network in agent and verifier phases with run-time SNI allowlist for the model endpoint only; explicit banned hosts (github, raw.githubusercontent, huggingface, zenodo, kaggle, azure blob) as held-out label sources; task-scoped API keys via harbor resolve_env_vars (a stray key is called out as a cheat vector on pinned-base-model tasks); grader runs the submission as an unprivileged uid with rlimits, staged copies, symlink/hardlink/size/TOCTOU checks, per-move timeouts, and bwrap namespaces in some tasks; sha256 pins on anchors and scorer; fail-closed zero reward on any invalid artifact, exception, or inconsistent reward files; prompt-level prohibitions (no hard-coding answers, no reading sealed set, preserve interface, respect stdlib/size caps); human 90+ item leakage/provenance rubric and trajectory audit per task. No anti-overfitting detection beyond the sealed split; no monitoring of agent behaviour during the run.

deep_reads.name: OpenClaw — Skill Workshop (proposal-gated self-authored skills) + plugin hook seam
deep_reads.mechanism:
OpenClaw is a personal-agent gateway (Node, TypeScript) that hosts model harnesses (its own loop, Codex app-server, Claude Code, Copilot) as plugins. Skill Workshop (shipped 2026.4.21, src/skills/workshop/, ~80 files) is its path for the agent to author/modify its own SKILL.md procedure files.

Governed path (`autonomous.mode: "propose"` or explicit chat/CLI/`/learn`): the agent calls the `skill_workshop` tool with `create|update|prepare_patch|patch|revise|evaluate|apply|reject|quarantine`. Output is stored as `PROPOSAL.md` under `<state>/skill-workshop/proposals/<id>/generations/<gen>/`, never as live SKILL.md. Each proposal record carries draftHash, revisionHash, target binding + target content hash, scanner state, support files (only under assets/examples/references/scripts/templates; executables, traversal, hidden segments rejected), and lives in SQLite with an append-only event ledger (`skills.proposals.events.list` with nextSequence). Update proposals bind to the live target hash; any drift flips them `stale`. `prepare_patch` issues a single-use exact-span authority bound to a read receipt; a runtime usage receipt restricts foreground repair to skills actually used that run.

`apply` (apply-transition.ts) is the only live write: it checks status==pending, expectedRevisionHash, draftHash, frontmatter, reruns the regex security scanner (critical -> quarantine), checks evaluation id and targetTreeSha256 under a mutation lock, writes rollback metadata (previous content + hashes) before touching files, then commits record+event atomically.

Plugins register `skill_proposal_evaluate` (receives immutable candidate bundle with file/tree hashes and baseline; returns findings/metrics/`pass|revise|block`), `skill_proposal_changed`, `skill_changed` (before/after tree hashes), and generic `before_tool_call` (block / requireApproval / params rewrite).

Ungoverned path (default `mode: "auto"`): a detached post-turn "experience review" (after >=10 model iterations, 30s idle) and a weekly per-agent cron "collection review" edit the Workshop directory directly with rooted file tools; no proposal, no scanner, no rollback snapshot.
deep_reads.eval_loop: There is no task-based or benchmark evaluation of whether a generated skill works. Acceptance = (1) regex security scanner (src/skills/security/scanner.ts, explicitly "no AST"): critical rules for child_process exec/eval, crypto-miner strings, process.env, prompt-injection phrases ("ignore previous instructions", "system prompt"), pipe-to-shell, env exfil; warn for rm -rf, chmod 777, base64 blobs; only critical blocks/quarantines; (2) hash/ownership/size checks; (3) optional plugin evaluators via `skill_proposal_evaluate` — none bundled, and timeouts/errors are recorded as attributed outcomes that do NOT block ("only a completed decision: block vetoes apply", i.e. fail-open); (4) human apply only if `approvalPolicy: "pending"` (default "auto" lets the agent call apply itself with no prompt). Learning decisions themselves are model-judged: "Every learning decision comes from a model reviewing real evidence." Usage tracking exists (`skill.used` events, `skills.curator.status`) but "no skill is archived or expired by age" and absence of use "never justifies removal". The docs state OpenClaw "does not schedule, auto-revise, or decide when such a loop should stop" — the optimization loop is deliberately left to external controllers.
deep_reads.limitations: (a) The governed path is opt-in: code default is `autonomous.mode: "auto"` + `approvalPolicy: "auto"` (config.ts DEFAULT_CONFIG). In auto mode, background experience review and weekly collection review use ordinary file tools: "Direct maintenance does not create proposals, run a post-turn scanner, or record automatic rollback snapshots"; "There is no collection-wide transaction, post-turn scanner, automatic rollback"; docs admit "Residual risk remains: an agent can make an incorrect edit." (b) Even in propose mode, agent-initiated apply runs "without an additional approval prompt by default". (c) The rule that foreground agents must go through `skill_workshop` "is advisory and prompt-enforced. The tool-policy seam does not enforce it." (d) Scanner is regex-only and safety-oriented; nothing checks correctness or quality. (e) Evaluators fail open on timeout/error; `correlationId` is "not authenticated identity or proof of authorization". (f) Scope is only the agent's own workshop-skills dir; bundled/plugin/ClawHub/workspace skills, config, prompts, and code use other paths. (g) Harness coverage is uneven: rooted reviews are "unsupported" for the Codex harness, undeclared CLI backends, node-placed CLI; sandboxed runs "do not construct the host-side Workshop proposal tool"; sandboxing and exec approvals are off by default. (h) Operational fragility in issues: #146023 rooted review inherited workspace bootstrap instructions and attempted out-of-root reads (jobs failed); #144515 no per-agent opt-out, reviews timing out 24-32 min; #141102 jobs shown enabled though deterministically rejected; #145723 stale proposals stuck with no cleanup; #145503 tool not registered after 9.3 migration; #146116/#144739 SQLite schema migration failures across 9.2->9.4. (i) No metrics anywhere on skill quality, acceptance rate, or regression.
deep_reads.key_insight: A proposal-first, hash-bound, event-ledgered gate for agent self-modification is buildable and ships at 389k-star scale — but the same project flipped its default to ungoverned direct edits ("auto"), showing that an acceptance layer must be cheap and autonomous-friendly or it gets bypassed by design; and the gate as shipped only checks safety (regex) and consistency (hashes), never whether the change actually works.
open_gaps: No verification that an applied skill improves task outcomes: no benchmark, replay, or regression test on the target procedure; only regex safety + hashes + optional model-graded evaluators.
Evaluators fail open (timeouts/errors are non-blocking); a harness-agnostic gate needs fail-closed semantics and authenticated evaluator identity, which OpenClaw explicitly leaves to plugins.

Default mode bypasses the gate entirely; there is no audit trail, diff, or rollback for auto-mode direct edits beyond generic backups — the acceptance layer has to cover the 'file tools' path, not just the tool-call path.
Gate scope is one artifact type (agent-owned SKILL.md); config changes, plugin installs, prompts, memory, and code edits each have separate, inconsistent approval mechanisms.

Harness dependence: rooted reviews and experience review only work where the runtime reports model/iteration/tool facts and enforces the root (embedded runner, Codex app-server); other CLI harnesses fail closed or are unsupported — evidence that harness-agnosticism requires a minimal runtime-facts contract.
Cross-agent verification: proposals are agent-scoped (#110940), so a supervising agent cannot review another agent's proposals through the same tool.
No usage-based or outcome-based retirement of skills ('every skill reports as active'), so bad skills accumulate until a model-judged weekly review removes them.
Multi-step external optimization loops are 'supported as primitives' but unimplemented and untested in-repo; no reference controller exists.
deep_reads.relevance_to_acceptance_layer:
Directly reusable design (verified in src/skills/workshop/): (1) Proposal as a first-class immutable object with draftHash, revisionHash, target-content hash, and targetTreeSha256, re-validated under a mutation lock at apply and flipped to `stale` on any drift — the correct shape for "accept exactly what was reviewed". (2) Atomic generation publish (write full bundle, rename, fsync parent dir, commit SQLite record + lifecycle event together) so interruption never yields a half-applied state. (3) Rollback metadata (previous content + hashes for skill and each support file) written before the live write. (4) Append-only event ledger with sequence cursors plus `expectedRevisionHash` and `correlationId` on every lifecycle action — an explicit API for an external controller to observe -> evaluate -> revise -> apply and to detect stale orchestration steps; the docs say outright that OpenClaw supplies these primitives and "does not automatically revise proposals or run an unbounded evaluation loop", which is exactly the slot a harness-agnostic acceptance layer would fill. (5) Evaluator envelope contract (`evaluatorVersion`, `mode: baseline-comparison`, `decision: pass|revise|block`, metrics, findings, 512 KiB cap, per-evaluator registrationId and timeout) and the candidate bundle with per-file hashes + tree hash + baseline. (6) Bounded write authorities: single-use exact-span `prepare_patch`, read receipts (`readSkillHashes`), runtime usage receipts, per-run proposal mutation budget, maxPending/maxSkillBytes caps, no-clobber and directory ownership rules. (7) `before_tool_call` seam semantics worth copying: `block:true` terminal, first `requireApproval` wins and freezes the param snapshot, approval timeouts leave state unchanged with an explicit "do not retry in a loop" reason.

What it proves: this class of gate is implementable in production with modest cost and survives migrations, restarts, and multi-harness hosting. What it disproves/warns: a gate that only checks safety and consistency is not an acceptance layer for RSI — nothing here tests that the modified skill produces better behavior; and the project's own default (`auto`) shows operators will trade the gate for autonomy, so the acceptance layer must be able to run autonomously (fast, deterministic, fail-closed) rather than depend on human apply. Evaluator fail-open, prompt-only enforcement of the tool path, and unsandboxed defaults are anti-patterns to avoid. Harness-agnosticism lesson: OpenClaw's gate only functions where the harness reports resolved model, iteration count, and tool availability and honors a rooted file surface ("changing the CLI working directory alone does not provide containment"); the Codex harness and node-placed CLIs are excluded. A harness-agnostic layer therefore needs a small mandatory runtime-facts + rooted-write contract as its adapter interface, and must also intercept the generic file-write path, not just a dedicated tool. Left open: outcome-based acceptance tests, authenticated evaluator identity, coverage of non-skill artifacts, and cross-agent review.
deep_reads.safety_measures: Proposal-only storage (PROPOSAL.md, never SKILL.md until apply); regex security scanner rerun at apply (critical -> quarantine; rules for child_process/eval/miners/process.env/prompt-injection phrases/pipe-to-shell/env exfil); literal-secret rejection; hash binding of update targets (stale on drift) and targetTreeSha256 revalidation under lock; rollback metadata before live write; atomic generation rename + fsync + single SQLite commit; append-only lifecycle ledger; support-file path rules (no absolute/traversal/hidden/executable/non-UTF-8, <=8 path components, 64 files, 256 KiB each/2 MiB total); size caps (40 KB body default, 200 KB ceiling, 10k chars for autonomous proposals, 160-byte description, maxPending 50); optional `approvalPolicy: "pending"` producing approval cards with 70s timeout (Codex 90s watchdog) that leave the proposal unchanged on expiry; per-run mutation budget and single-use prepare_patch authority; runtime usage receipt limiting repair to skills used; background reviews run under detached session identity, inherit source permissions, file tools rooted at the Workshop dir, fail closed when runtime facts or root enforcement are unavailable, one attempt no retry; Gateway methods scoped to operator.admin for mutations; Doctor reconciliation for stale/missing drafts and migrations. Explicit non-guarantees: auto-mode direct edits have no scanner/rollback/transaction; sandboxing and exec approvals off by default; native plugins run in-process unsandboxed; foreground tool-path rule is prompt-enforced only.

deep_reads.name: Hermes Agent (Nous Research)
deep_reads.mechanism:
Hermes is a general-purpose Python agent (CLI/TUI, Telegram/Discord/Slack gateway, desktop app) whose "learning loop" is a set of prompt-driven background forks that write to two stores: SKILL.md packages under ~/.hermes/skills/ (procedural memory, agentskills.io-compatible) and MEMORY.md/USER.md (declarative, hard-capped ~2.2K/1.4K chars).

Post-turn background review (agent/background_review.py, agent/turn_finalizer.py): after every completed turn, if the turn used >= skills.creation_nudge_interval tool iterations (default 10) or memory.nudge_interval turns (default 10), a daemon-thread clone of the agent replays the conversation snapshot with a fixed prompt ("Be ACTIVE - most sessions produce at least one skill update... a pass that does nothing is a missed learning opportunity"). Preference order: patch a loaded skill > patch an umbrella > add references/templates/scripts > create a class-level skill. Fork limits: 16 iterations, 600K input-token budget, dispatch-side whitelist (skills toolset, memory tool only on memory triggers, read_file/search_files; write_file/patch/terminal denied), dangerous commands auto-denied, cancelled by the next live turn. Enabled by default, fail-open. Same model/credentials as parent for prompt-cache parity.

skill_manage tool (tools/skill_manager_tool.py + skill_manager_guards.py): create/edit/patch/delete/write_file/remove_file. Hard checks: YAML frontmatter with name+description, 60-char description budget on create, size cap, name uniqueness. Advisory linter never blocks. Opt-in (default off) regex security scan and skills.write_approval staging (/skills pending|diff|approve|reject). Every mutation is appended to a JSONL ledger with content-addressed before/after blobs and single-entry rollback ("TELEMETRY, NOT A GATE"). Background-origin writes (ContextVar provenance) are refused on pinned, bundled, hub, external, and any skill lacking created_by:agent; read-before-write is enforced; deletes require absorbed_into=<existing umbrella>.

Curator (agent/curator.py): inactivity-triggered (7d interval, 2h idle), deterministic active->stale(14d)->archived(30d) transitions, never deletes; opt-in LLM consolidation pass builds umbrella skills. /learn distills user-named sources into a skill; /journey renders learned skills+memory as a graph; /review spawns an independent reviewer subagent on demand. Companion repo hermes-agent-self-evolution (DSPy+GEPA, Phase 1 skill evolution only, dormant since 2026-06) evolves SKILL.md offline behind test/size/PR-review gates.
deep_reads.eval_loop: There is no closed evaluation loop on the learning loop itself. Skill creation/patching is accepted on the writing model's own judgment plus prompt heuristics ("do not capture" lists, class-level naming rules); nothing executes, replays, or A/B-tests a new skill before it becomes live and loaded into future system prompts. Curator archival is driven by usage timestamps (.usage.json use_count/last_used_at), not outcome quality. The evals/ directory (~150 files) contains infra probes (compaction scorecards, browser_use tasks, core_tool_deferral, postmortem forensics) but no benchmark measuring whether agent-created skills improve later task success. The companion hermes-agent-self-evolution repo has real gates (full pytest suite, size limits, semantic preservation, human PR merge) but is offline, Phase-1-only, and stalled since June 2026. The "40% faster with 20+ self-created skills" figure circulating in third-party blogs is attributed to "Nous internal benchmarks" and does not appear in the repo, docs, or release notes; treat as unverified.
deep_reads.limitations: Author, executor, and judge are the same model (issue #25833, P2, needs-decision). Documented real failures: transient env failures persisted as durable skills causing tool avoidance ("learned helplessness", #6051, fixed only by prompt text); the background reviewer canonicalized a hallucinated empty-directory finding as a skill after the user had refuted it in-session; session-specific ports generalized into global rules; the curator archived 10 operational skills in one pass with zero verified consolidations (#29912); ledger rollback restored a hollow skill (#96962); an agent aggressively rewrote a user's weeks-of-work skill (#41939); a tool-denial storm (~142 denials + ~204 read-before-write refusals over 2 days) silently starved the loop so almost no patch landed (#61521); guard "allowed-exactly-once" race (#67140); fork token usage invisible to telemetry (#87250); local LLMs spend 2-3 min generating skills per review (#12340). Skill dedup is name-only; no usage-tracked lifecycle beyond timestamps; skills.guard_agent_created and write_approval default off; fail-open defaults throughout. Review-time cost ~30K tokens/event. Repo velocity (947 commits in 4 days, 42.8K open issues, heavy automated triage) makes any given code path unstable.
deep_reads.key_insight: Hermes is the largest deployed example of an agent that autonomously rewrites its own procedural memory, and its issue tracker is a field catalogue of what goes wrong when acceptance is delegated to the writing model: the safeguards that actually held up in production were all mechanism-level (write-origin provenance, ownership/pin guards, read-before-write, ledger+rollback, staged approval, absorbed_into fail-closed deletes), while every prompt-level quality rule was eventually bypassed or over-applied.
open_gaps: No verification that a created/patched skill is correct: no isolated dry-run, replay, or reproducibility check before it goes live (#25833, #416 still open)
No outcome-based scoring: curator lifecycle uses timestamps, not success rate; no per-skill success_rate/consistency metadata
No content-addressed skill versioning or receipts tying an output to the skill version that produced it (#11692 proposes Ed25519 decision receipts; only external skeleton repos exist)
No meta-authorization model for self-modification scope (which domains, how many mutations per window) - only binary write_approval
Security scan of agent-created skills defaults off (#16461); write_approval defaults off; background review fail-open
Name-only duplicate detection; semantic overlap left to the opt-in LLM curator pass
No pre-emit claim verification or auditor hook contract (#26742, needs-decision)
Rollback granularity is per-ledger-entry and has had completeness bugs; no atomic multi-entry transaction rollback
Fork token cost partly invisible; no budget accounting for the learning loop across sessions
Self-evolution companion (GEPA) never wired into the runtime loop; Phases 2-5 unimplemented
deep_reads.relevance_to_acceptance_layer:
Directly relevant as both a reference implementation and a negative-result corpus. Reusable pieces (all MIT, mostly self-contained modules): (1) tools/skill_provenance.py - a ContextVar write-origin ("foreground" vs "background_review") that lets guards apply stricter policy to unattended actors; this is the cleanest harness-agnostic primitive here and maps directly onto an acceptance layer's "who is proposing this change" axis. (2) tools/skill_manager_guards.py - ownership (created_by:agent only), pin, external/bundled/hub refusal, read-before-write (must load exact target in the same review turn), and fail-closed delete requiring a verified forwarding target; each was added after a concrete production incident, so the guard set is empirically motivated. (3) tools/skill_ledger.py - JSONL mutation ledger with sha256 content-addressed before/after manifests and rollback_entry that fails closed if the safety capture fails; a good base for a change-record format, though it is explicitly telemetry, not a gate. (4) tools/write_approval + /skills pending|diff|approve|reject - a staged-write pattern that survives restarts and replays approved payloads through the same tool with a gate-bypass token; this is the shape a harness-agnostic acceptance layer should expose. (5) Curator's structured YAML summary (consolidations/prunings) reconciled against actual tool calls (_reconcile_classification) - a pattern for cross-checking an LLM's self-report against the ledger. (6) hermes-agent-self-evolution's gate list (tests, size, cache compatibility, semantic preservation, human PR) as an offline acceptance checklist.

What it proves: prompt-level quality rules ("do not capture transient failures", "class-level names only") do not prevent contamination; the incidents in #6051/#25833/#29912/#41939 all happened with those rules present. Provenance-scoped, fail-closed, tool-level guards are what stopped recurrence. It also proves the loop can silently starve (denial storm) - an acceptance layer must expose rejection telemetry, not just block.

What it disproves: that a busy, well-resourced project will add verification on its own - #416 (validation) has been open since March 2026 and #25833 is marked needs-decision.

What it leaves open for the acceptance layer: any behavioral verification of a proposed skill (dry-run in isolation, replay against held-out sessions, regression against the previously loaded version), content-addressed skill versions with output-to-version receipts, scoped meta-authorization for self-modification, outcome-based lifecycle scoring, and cross-harness portability of the guard/ledger contract (everything here is bound to Hermes' skill_manage tool and ~/.hermes layout). Hermes' write_approval JSON payloads and ledger entries are the natural integration points for an external gate.
deep_reads.safety_measures: Write-origin provenance ContextVar; background-review write guard (pinned, bundled, hub, external-dir, protected built-ins, non-curator-managed skills all refused; fail-closed when provenance unreadable); read-before-write enforced per review turn; curator delete requires absorbed_into=<existing umbrella>; curator never deletes, only archives to .archive/ with snapshot backup/rollback; per-mutation JSONL ledger with content-addressed blobs and rollback; opt-in skills.write_approval and memory.write_approval staging with human approve/reject; opt-in skills.guard_agent_created regex scanner (default off); advisory linter; Skills Guard trust-tiered scan on hub installs plus optional NVIDIA SkillEvaluator/SkillSpector advisory scan; review fork tool whitelist (no write_file/patch/terminal), 16-iteration cap, 600K input-token budget, dangerous commands auto-denied, cancelled by next live turn, idle-deferred on managed local runtimes; curator first-run deferral and dry-run mode; pinned skills exempt from all autonomous action; cron-referenced skills protected; self_repo_guard blocks git operations that would rewrite the running checkout; command approval/allowlist system for terminal.
deep_reads.key_results: No quantitative results for the learning loop in the repository or docs. Scale signals: 245,205 stars, 51,017 forks, 42,817 open issues, 760+ contributors on v0.21.0; v0.21.2 (tag v2026.9.11, 2026-09-11) rolled up 947 commits/312 PRs in four days. Codebase: ~6,200 Python files, ~4,230 test files (25+ test modules cover background_review/curator/ledger), 58 bundled skills. Documented operational numbers from issues: ~30K tokens per review event; denial storm of ~142 denials + ~204 refusals over 2 days on one deployment; 10 operational skills archived in a single bad curator pass. Third-party "40% faster with 20+ skills" claim is unsourced.
deep_reads.venue_or_citations: Open-source repo (MIT); no paper. Companion hermes-agent-self-evolution (5,327 stars) builds on GEPA (ICLR 2026 Oral is the GEPA paper, not Hermes). Widely covered by blogs; cited in community proposals for signed decision receipts (IETF draft-farley-acta-signed-receipts, in-toto Decision Receipt predicate).

deep_reads.name: lobehub/awesome-rsi (Awesome RSI: A curated research map of Recursive Self-Improvement)
deep_reads.mechanism:
This is a reference map, not a system: a single 59 KB README (226 link entries; 141 arXiv, 37 GitHub) under the LobeHub org, CC0-licensed, maintained by one person (MaxForAI, sole CODEOWNER, 36 of 48 commits; early commits authored as MaLiu1999). Created 2026-08-11, populated in a burst on 2026-08-16/17, then extended via ~15 merged community PRs.

Structure: (1) a Scope & Terminology block that operationally separates self-refinement (no persistent change), persistent self-improvement (weights/memory/skills/prompts/harness/code carry forward), recursive self-improvement (the improvement mechanism is itself the object of improvement), and RSI substrate (exposes structure but no loop by default); (2) taxonomy by update surface: Model-level (self-training, synthetic data, self-play, self-taught reasoning), Harness-level (prompt/program optimization, context/memory evolution, harness/scaffold evolution, extensible substrates, self-verification foundations, self-evolving frameworks), Multi-agent, Coding/SWE self-modification, Automated AI R&D, Embodied, Evolutionary/open-ended, Safety/Alignment/Theory, Introspection, Benchmarks (direct RSI evals / frontier-lab frameworks / AI R&D proxies / agent proxies), Frameworks & Tools, blogs, talks.

Admission process is the distinctive part: every PR/issue must answer six questions — what is improved, does it persist across iterations, is the improvement mechanism itself subject to improvement, why RSI-specific, publication status, public artifacts plus an Open/Partial/Internal/NA evaluation-artifact classification. Benchmarks are admitted only if they measure a bottleneck constraining persistent/recursive improvement. CI is awesome-lint@2.3.0 on every PR/push and a weekly lychee external-link check (openai.com, lesswrong, openreview, sciencedirect excluded). Ordering rules: newest year first, alphabetical within year.

Observed curation behavior: rejected FrontierCS (#10) as a general capability benchmark; demanded a resolvable primary source for Tricog (#21); required template completion and a precisely bounded description for RecurSE (#20); merged Reef (#22) after the submitter explicitly disclosed it is persistent, not recursive, self-improvement; forced an 8-paper batch PR (#25) to be split into one-per-PR.
deep_reads.eval_loop: No experimental evaluation — it is a bibliography. Its own quality loop is: awesome-lint on PR/push, weekly external link check, single-maintainer review against the six-question RSI rubric. Spot-checks of two acceptance-relevant entries against the primary sources found the one-sentence descriptions accurate: SkillOpt (arXiv 2605.23904) does accept an edit 'only when it strictly improves a held-out validation score' with a textual learning-rate budget and rejected-edit buffer (+23.5/+24.8/+19.1 pp on GPT-5.5 across chat/Codex/Claude Code, best-or-tied in 52/52 cells, code at aka.ms/skillopt); Agentic Harness Engineering (arXiv 2604.25850) does pair every harness edit with a self-declared prediction verified on the next round ('falsifiable contracts'), Terminal-Bench 2 pass@1 69.7 -> 77.0 over ten iterations vs human-designed Codex-CLI 71.9, +5.1 to +10.1 pp cross-family transfer. Open issue #14 (audit artifact availability of every benchmark entry, add [Open]/[Partial]/[Internal] markers) has had zero activity since 2026-08-24.
deep_reads.limitations: Single maintainer and single-org bus factor; 11 PRs opened 2026-09-11/12 sit unreviewed. One-sentence descriptions restate abstracts and are not verified results — 64 of 226 entries are 2026 arXiv preprints and 35 are 2025, so much of the map is unreviewed claims. Some weak inclusions: RSI-Bench is listed under 'Direct RSI Evaluations' yet has 1 star and no activity since 2026-03; frontier-lab evaluation entries (OpenAI RSI Index, Anthropic AI R&D-4, GDM FSF) point to internal suites that cannot be rerun. No acceptance/verification/gating category exists: SkillOpt, AHE, DGM, autoresearch, Reef, AI4AI-at-Scale, LongWoF-Bench each embed a bespoke gate but are scattered across five sections and never compared. Artifact-availability markers promised in CONTRIBUTING are not yet displayed. Coverage gaps: the R-Zero/G-Zero/VisPlay/TTCS co-evolution family is pending in open PRs; no entries on statistical validity of accept/reject decisions, eval contamination by the evolving agent, or protection of the gate from self-modification. Smaller than competitors (ANative-Lab/Awesome-Self-Evolving-Agents 2482 stars, CharlesQ9/Self-Evolving-Agents 1318, selfimproving-agent list 478) though those are staler.
deep_reads.key_insight: The list's own admission rubric — what is improved, what carries forward, whether the improvement mechanism itself changes, and whether evaluation artifacts are Open/Partial/Internal — is a cleaner per-change acceptance schema than most self-improving systems it catalogs, and the absence of any acceptance/verification section in a 226-entry RSI map is direct evidence that gating remains bespoke and unshared across the field.
open_gaps: No taxonomy node for acceptance gates, promotion/rollback, or verification of self-modifications; the relevant systems (SkillOpt, Agentic Harness Engineering, DGM, autoresearch, Reef, AI4AI at Scale, LongWoF-Bench) are scattered across five sections and never compared on gate design
Question 3 of the rubric asks whether the improvement mechanism evolves but never asks whether the evaluator/acceptance gate is protected from modification by the evolving agent

No entries on statistical validity of accept decisions (noise, multiple comparisons, small held-out sets) or on evaluation contamination/Goodharting of the gate by the agent being gated, beyond theory-level sandbagging and reward-tampering papers
Artifact-availability audit (issue #14) never executed; benchmark entries lack [Open]/[Partial]/[Internal] markers despite CONTRIBUTING defining them
Frontier-lab RSI evaluation entries are non-reproducible internal suites; no open harness-agnostic RSI evaluation with adoption exists (RSI-Bench has 1 star)
Single maintainer; 11 PRs from 2026-09-11/12 unreviewed; co-evolution/zero-data family (R-Zero, G-Zero, MM-Zero, VisPlay, TTCS) and DRACO credit-assignment work still pending
Descriptions are abstract paraphrases; no per-entry demonstrated-vs-claimed annotation or headline numbers
deep_reads.relevance_to_acceptance_layer: Bears on the acceptance-layer project as a map and a schema, not as a mechanism. Reuse directly: (a) the Scope & Terminology ladder (self-refinement / persistent / recursive / substrate) as the axis that decides what an acceptance layer must gate — a change that does not persist needs no gate, a change to the mechanism that produces changes needs a stronger gate; (b) the six-question admission rubric maps almost one-to-one onto per-change metadata a harness-agnostic gate should require: target surface (weights/prompt/memory/skill/harness/code), what artifact carries forward, whether the change touches the improvement mechanism itself, and Open/Partial/Internal reproducibility status of the evidence; (c) its pointers to the concrete gates already in the field: SkillOpt (strict held-out improvement, edit budget, rejected-edit buffer), Agentic Harness Engineering (self-declared prediction per edit, falsified or confirmed next round), DGM (empirical validation plus archive instead of proofs), karpathy/autoresearch (keep only if val bits-per-byte improves), Reef (evaluate-then-promote with versioned artifacts and rollback; explicitly persistent-not-recursive), AI4AI at Scale (verification-gated loop banking accepted and rejected attempts as auditable experience), LongWoF-Bench (verifier-confirmed trajectory provenance), and the safety side (SAHOO goal-drift/constraint-preservation/regression-risk checks, Misevolution across model/memory/tool/workflow, synthetic-data verification against collapse, sandbagging). What it proves: every acceptance gate in the field is bespoke and coupled to one system; none is harness-agnostic, and the list has no category for one, which validates the gap this project targets. What it leaves open: no coverage of gate integrity (can the agent edit its own gate), statistical soundness of accept decisions, eval contamination, or standardized rollback semantics — these are the areas where an acceptance layer would be genuinely new rather than a re-packaging of SkillOpt/AHE/Reef gates. Practical use: treat the README as the seed corpus for a gate-design comparison table, and adopt its rubric as the change-manifest schema.
deep_reads.safety_measures: As a list: CC0 license, awesome-lint and weekly link-check CI, primary-source requirement, artifact-availability classification, single CODEOWNER review. Content-wise it has a 20-entry Safety/Alignment/Theory section (SAHOO drift monitoring, Misevolution, TamperBench, goal drift, self-modification theory, reward tampering, sandbagging, sleeper agents, safe interruptibility) but no operational guidance on gating self-modifications.
